THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with
David Albert Francis
Reel 1
Interview by Milt Hinton

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS

I am with David "Panama" Francis, and this is yours truly, Milt Hinton, rapping. We're around here in Nice, France, at the jazz festival. Panama, we want to talk about you here, on this Oral History, which is about your life. Now your name is David "Panama" Francis -- give me your real name.

It's David Albert Francis. I didn't get the name Panama until I came to New York in 1938, and I joined Roy Eldridge's band. I came to rehearsal for the first time with a Panama hat on; I'd just come from Florida, and that was what they were wearing down there at that time during the summer.

And something happened at rehearsal, and Roy -- I guess he didn't remember my name, although his name was David, too. He looked around and said to me, "Hey, Panama!" And the fellows in the band thought that was my name, and I was so afraid not to tell them it wasn't my name, because I was so happy to be in the band, that I just accepted it.
So ever since then, that's been it -- Panama.
All right. You were born when?
I was born December 21st, 1918 in Miami, Florida.
Uh huh. In the land of Down in Miami, Florida, huh?
Uh huh. December 21, 1918.
And your mother's name?
My mother's name was Hattie Jemaima Morrison -- that was her maiden name.
And your dad's name?

It was Louis Cloris Francis. Actually, the family name was Francoise, and when my father landed in Miami, Florida, whoever it was that had his papers, wrote down "Francis", and so ever since then, the name has been Francis, but actually the family name was Francoise. Because my father was Haitian.
Yeah, you said when your father landed in Miami -- I want to know where did he come from. Your parents were what?
My father's home was in Port au Prince, Haiti, and my mother was from Nassau in the Bahamas.

And my mother had been married before, and her husband died when my sister was about 4 years old, and then she came to Miami in 1916, I think, and my father left Haiti and went to Nassau first, and then came to Miami also around 1916.
Uh huh. So your mother met your father in Miami, then?
Yeah, in Miami.
Had they known one another?
No, they hadn't known each other before then. It was just like the present day time -- they
had a big revolution in Haiti, and my father was one of those that escaped because his family was pretty well off in Haiti, so they had to leave the country during the revolution over there.
You mentioned that your mother had been married before, and that she had had a daughter. What was her name -- your half sister -- what was her name?
Iona Roker.
Iona Roker. And that was in 1918 -- so were you the first born to your father?
To my father, yeah. The first born.
Were there any other children after you?
Yeah -- in fact, in three years and nine months time, my mother had three babies.
Oh boy.
Yeah. My father was working pretty hard!
Yeah? Well, what were those kids' names?
Well, my sister was named Naomi, and my brother was named Louis after my father -- he was a junior.
I think I met both your mother
and father, because I think I met your mother in Miami when we were with Cab Calloway. (Inaudible.)
Yeah.
How about your brothers and sisters? Are they still with us, Panama?
No. My sister, Naomi, she passed on when she was three years old from diphtheria. And my brother Louis is still alive, though; he's in Miami.
I remember Louis. Uh huh.
Now there was another sister that was born in 1928, and she died, too -- at childbirth.
Oh, I see. Uh huh.
In Miami, do you remember the first school or the early schools you went to there?

Yeah. The first grade school I remember going to was Miss Powell's School, and then I went to another private school that was run by Reverend Allen's church. I forgot the name of the professor, you know? Because there was one professor, and he had all of the grades -- he taught from the ABC's on, you know?
Uh huh. Talk about your early influence with music. What was the first influence in listening to music, and how you got interested in it?
Well, my father was a record collector. I remember one night when my sister Naomi was alive -- as young
as we were, I remember she and I playing the Victrola which "His Master's Voice" was one of the High Boy Victor things with the megaphone and and the dog on it?
Uh huh.

Well, I was climbing up one day to play a record -- I don't remember what record it was -- and I slipped and burst my lip. And my father went out and bought another Victrola which was the low type, because I guess he didn't want me to kill myself trying to play these records.

But the first record I remember playing was Ferde Grofé, a one-face record by Freddie Grofé, I think, orchestra, and " it was the tune Running Wild," and it was sung by a woman -- the only name they had on the record was Miss Virginia.
Virginia, huh?
Miss Virginia; that's the vocalist's name, and it was a record called "Running Wild" on the Victor label, if I remember correctly.
Uh huh. What were some of the first orchestras around town that you remember?
Well, I had a cousin of mine who was a trumpet player -- my cousin Harold, Harold Newchurch, and he used to play all the house parties around Miami.
Oh? What was his instrument? Piano?
Trumpet. He was a trumpet player.
How was he your cousin?

He was my cousin on my mother's side. I only met one of my father's relatives, and that was when I was with Cab Calloway when we played in Haiti, and I met one of my cousins who was a Senator there at the time.
Uh huh.
But my cousin, Harold Newchurch was my mother's first cousin; his mother and my grandfather were sister and brother, so he was my mother's first cousin, and he's my second cousin.
Oh, sure.

And during those days, they used to play the house parties, and most of the musicians, they just played for fun, because they had jobs they worked at during the day, and they played the parties there for, like, drinks and whatever the host felt like paying them, you know?
Oh yeah.

And that's one reason why my father, up until the day he died, he never felt a musician was worth anything, because he always looked back on my cousin Harold where all he would do was drink whiskey and have a good time!
There are a lot of people who have that same idea [even now!]
That's beautiful.
Yeah.
Now what were some of these bands?
Did you ever have any local bands around there?
Oh yeah. They had the Honey Boys around that time; that was a band that played at the Della Robia Ballroom, and at the time ...
The Della Robia Ballroom?
Yeah, the Della Robia Ballroom, and at the time -- and which later became the Rockland Palace.
Oh yeah, that was on Second Avenue, wasn't it?

Second Avenue between 8th and 9th Street. Well, I remember I had another cousin who was still alive in Miami who was a banjo player -- they called him The Ghost. His name was Preston Marshall. Now I have to explain this to you -- in my mother's family, my grandmother came from Exuma.
Exuma? Where's that?
Exuma -- that's one of the islands in Nassau. And my grandfather was born in Nassau, but he used to travel around the different islands, and that was when he met my grandmother.

And so I have one side of the family as my grandfather's side, and the other side of the family is my grandmother's side. So my cousin Harold is on my grandfather's side, and my cousin Preston is on my grandmother's side, so that's the Exuma side of the family -- and then there's the Nassau side of the family. They're all messed up!

A lot of soul brothers have that kind of thing. I can remember hearing my grandmother say things like that -- "Now this is your cousin Suzie, on your Aunt Mary's side, and this is your cousin Joe on ..." and you really get all mixed up there.

Well, that's the way it went down. Because, you know, I don't know anything about my great grandfather on my grandmother's side, but my great grandfather on my father's side was an ex-slave from South Carolina, and they stole a boat, and that's how they got to Nassau.
All right!
Yeah. Actually, the family originated in South Carolina.
That's really interesting, Panama. (Interruption) We were talking about some of the first bands that you ran into down there that influenced you. How did you become interested in drums?

Well, I tell you -- ever since I could remember, I wanted to play the drums. My mother told me that I used to sit down at the table, after eating, and I would take my spoon and beat on the table with it, and I could remember when I was around 4 or 5 years of age, they asked me what I wanted Santa Clause to bring me, and I told them a drum.
And I think every Christmas after that, I got
a drum, because that's all I was interested in -- having a drum.

And I was what you would call a very lonely child as far as my childhood went, because my sister, who was 8 years my senior, was actually who I would call my real mother, because like I said earlier, in three years and 9 months time, there were three babies in the house, and I was the oldest one -- so I don't ever remember my mother ever putting her arms around me or kissing me.
I was like, you know -- like they used to say, I used to sit down alone by myself and just look in to space, and people could be talking to me, and I wouldn't hear a word they said, you know?

I remember the first time being in a play -- I was about 5 years old, I think, in a church play, and I became terrified with the speech I was going to make, and I learned the speech and I knew it by heart, but for some reason, I just became so terrified, and I think that's the first time I ever remember stammering.

Up until that time, I don't ever remember stuttering. I started stuttering from that time on; I remember my mother and father, they both were so embarrassed and they gave me hell about it because I stood up there and froze. This is when I first remember started stuttering.
And from them on, I was always like a loner, you know?

I was always by myself, and the only consolation I had was my drum. That is something that I feel very close to me; I mean like my drum is like my right arm or my legs or my head -- that's how I feel about the drums, because they were the only companions I had.

My mother was very strict, and I remember that I was always told I wasn't a good boy, and I always tried to please her. Everyone in Miami who knows me knows that I never gave my mother any problems, or my father, any problems.

But it was, I think, something about my mother that she was ill, because she wasn't too nice to my sister or me, and all of the love that she should have shared between the three children was shared on just one - that was my brother.

So it wasn't what you would call a very nice childhood for me. But I do remember when I was 8 years old, I joined the Drum and Bugle Corps at the UNIA, and I couldn't read any music, but I could hear. I could hear something just one time, and I could play it on the drum. Drum and
So I was like the youngest one in the Bugle Corps; all the other kids were 11 and 12 years old, you know?
Yeah, I see.
So I went from there to the UNIA band, which is the UNiversal Negro Improvement Association, Marcus Garvey.
The UN-- what was that again?
UNIA.
UNIA.
The UNIA -- Universal Negro Improvement Association, which was founded by Marcus Garvey.
Yeah, we had that in Chicago, too.
Yeah?
And we also had an Ancient Knights and Daughters of Africa.

That's really interesting, because the things are similar -- black people were starting to get together all over the country. This great man, Marcus Garvey was really one of the first real great organizers, don't you think?
Yeah, I think so. He really got us on the right track.
He sure did.
The only sad part about it is that he was a foreigner and a lot of people turned against him, because of that.
Right.

But after that, I joined the UNIA band. I played the drum there with an older man -- his name was McCullough, Mr. David McCullough. He's an ex army man, and he played the drum in the army. And I still wasn't able to read, but I could play all the marches, like the Sousa marches, and things, and so I used to play the parades around there.
Uh huh.
So when I got to be around 10 years

old, there was a church on Fifth Court and 17th Street, the Church of God and Christ, and I played the drum there on Sundays with a man that he played at the time, I didn't know it was a cello, because we called it a base, but he played the base on the cello, and his son played the piano, and I played the drum.
And the sisters in the church had the tambourine, and one of them played the bass drum. I played the snare, and this was my job on Sundays -- I used to get 50¢ for playing at the church on Sundays.
Beautiful. That is most interesting. But there is one thing I'd just like to clear up while we're on your early childhood. About your parents. They evidently separated at some time, didn't they?

Yes, they did. They separated, but during my early childhood, there never was any happiness in the house, I remember my mother was an extremely jealous woman, and my father was very outgoing, and there were always arguments going on, so he was out of the house most of the time -- he was never home. He just came home, probably, after work and ate his dinner and probably went back out again, because he loved to play cards, and he'd be playing with his friends.
So almost all of my childhood was spent mostly with my mother.
I know he came to New York.
Yeah. Well, they separated when I was 11. I was working up to that; I was coming up to that.
You were coming up to that?

Yeah. See, while I was playing with the UNIA band, most of the large churches had their own marching bands, like St. Agnes Church, which was one of the biggest Episcopal churches in Miami for black people, they had their own band -- the St. Agnes Cornet Band, and the guy that was the leader of that band was a guy from Nassau by the name of Roberts, but everybody called him Bella Roberts -- he was a great trumpet player.
And one day he came by the house, and asked my mother if I could join the St. Agnes Band as a drummer, so here I was, 11 years old, playing in the St. Agnes Marching Band.
That's interesting. So did you finally join the St. Agnes Church, for religion? What was your religion?
No. I belonged to St. Peter's American Catholic Church.
Aha. So your religion was Catholic then.
Yes, Catholic. I was Catholic.
Yeah, that was quite apropos for the Caribbean, too.
Oh yeah, my father being from Haiti and all, they are all Catholics anyway.
Uh huh.

But the reason why he left the Roman Catholic Church was because after he joined the Garvey movement, the Garvey movement had a church that they started of their own, and they made it the American Catholic Church, so that's how I became a member of that church.
But I was really christened in the Roman Catholic Church. Downtown. They had a section in the Roman Catholic Church downtown for blacks when I was born, and that's where I was christened at.
Again, what did your dad do for a living? What kind of a job did he have in Florida?
Well, I tell you. My father started out as a construction worker, and he eventually ended up a spiritualist around Miami -- that's what he did.

Yeah. How was conditions then for you, you know? I know I go back a little further than you -- 1910, but always the black people were on the low end of the totem pole, of course, but was your father able to make a pretty good living so that there was enough ... you know?
Yeah, my father made a very good living. But one of the reasons why this happened with him was because of him being able to speak a foreign language, and
he spoke English with a heavy French accent -- that he was not an ordinary nigger, he was a different kind of nigger, you know what I'm saying?
Yeah -- I got you.

So that's the reason why a lot -- like there were a lot of stores that my father was able to go into, and shop that blacks couldn't go into, and the only reason that happened was because he spoke a language, it made him different -- even though he was as black as me. And you'd know him, you saw him.
Sure, that's right.
Yeah, and that made the difference.
He was quite a handsome man. I think he kind of beat you there.
Yeah, I guess that was why my mother was so jealous.
Oh, yeah, he was really something. A real handsome man.
Yeah.
So you had it pretty cool there growing up, as far as that was concerned, then?

Oh yeah. I don't remember having any hungry days or things like that, because my father was, you know -- in fact, I remember that my father was the kind of man who wouldn't allow my mother to work or buy her own clothes. Why, he used to buy material and take it to the
dressmaker to make dresses for my mother -- I remember, I remember these things, you know?
Beautiful ...

But now, all during this time, I was still listening to records, you know; as I told you, from an early age -- my father used to collect records -- Butterfield and Ma Rainey, Beans and Suzie, and Bessie Smith, and Gene Austin -- he came to Miami I think in 1926, and had a big turnout there for him, you know?
Uh huh.
But Miami was not the nicest town in the world then, you know? Miami was very bad -- they had their lynchings and everything there, just like everywhere else in the south.
But Second Avenue was the black street there, though, wasn't it?

Well, Second Avenue was the main drag for blacks, say, from 6th Street back to 11th Street -- that was where everything happened. I remember after I became like a teenager, you could stand on the corner of Second Avenue and 8th Street and see everybody that lived in Miami on a Saturday, starting around twelve o'clock, everybody was going downtown to shop, and they always came up Second Avenue. You got the chance to see everybody that you knew, you know?
I think the ballroom was there ...
Yeah, the ballroom, the theatre -- the Rich Theatre and the Lyric Theatre; that's where all the shows used to come at one time, at the Lyric Theatre.
Yeah, and they had some good restaurants.
Oh, yeah; they had the Boston Chop House, Salina's Tea Room, and Bill Rivers had a restuarant there.
Right. What was the name of that place Bill Rivers owned?
He owned the Rockland Palace, which was originally the Della Robia.
Right, that's right. Hey, that's beautiful, man. What were some of the first bands that you got to play with, I mean, like getting into jazz?

Well, I got into jazz playing house parties. Yeah. See, they used to have a lot of house parties in Miami, I mean, everybody used to give a party there on a Saturday, and so that was how I got the chance to start playing house parties.
I think my first party I played was with Bubba Roberts on trumpet, his daughter, Gladys played piano, and a guy named, Milton Fletcher -- he was on bass.
Yeah, Milton Fletcher.
Right, Milton Fletcher on bass, and
I played the drum. That was my first gig. I remember I was about 11 years old when I played that party.
What was Roberts' first name?
Hubert.
But you called him Bubba?
No, Bella. Bella. That's the West Indian name for 'brother'. Instead of saying brother, they say 'bella'.
That's great, really -- Bella Roberts, eh?

Yep, Bella Roberts. So that was my first time that I remember playing. But then my mother found out that I had a natural talent for the drums, and at this time, they had separated -- they separated when I was around 11 years old. And that's when I became the meal ticket.
Uh huh.

Because I remember my first well-paying job -- I was around 12 going on 13, I played at a place on Third Avenue and 14th Street at the Barbecue Stand. That was one of those places where somebody either got killed or cut up or stabbed, during the night. And ...
Especially on the weekend.
Yeah, on the weekend, yeah. I used to work there four nights a week. Wednesday, Thursday,

Friday and Saturday. And I always have a soft spot in my heart for upright pianos. Because there were many a night when they started shooting, the whole band went behind the piano at the time, because they felt that the wood in the piano being so thick, that the bullet wouldn't come through -- which many times, we would hear the strings saying 'ping' because the bullet had hit the string, and you know ...
And we'd be all behind the piano, stooping down.
Uh huh.
So I played at this place for about six months -- my mother would take me there and sit and wait for me to bring me home at night.
Then, when I was going on 14, that's when I joined Little George Kelly and his Cavaliers.
The George Kelly we know?
Yeah, the George Kelly we know, in a local band -- a bunch of teenaged kids. Teenagers. But they had this little band, George Kelly and his Cavaliers.
Yeah? That's beautiful.
Because the top band at that time in Miami was Hartley Toots.
Oh yeah, I remember that band.
Yeah, and his Orange Pickers.
Uh huh. Name some of the guys who were in that band with George Kelly -- some of the guys that
you remember being in that band with George.

Well, let's see now -- there was Ernest Thompson, who later on played with Louis Armstrong, played baritone saxophone -- baritone -- with Louis Armstrong. There was Vincent Oliveri, there was Maurice Meadows was another trumpet player; there was a guy named Arthur Duncan who is now a big AAME minister in Montgomery, Alabama.
Wow.

He has a big church there in Montgomeryere. There ws also a guy who played trombone we called 'Foots' - but he died very young. I can't remember Foots' real name. And then in the saxophone section, there was George Kelly, George McCaskel --
What did George McCaskel play -- alto or tenor?

Alto, he played alto. George, and the other alto player was a guy named Mr. Higgs, who was also a schoolteacher in Miami at the time. Mr. Higgs, yeah, he played the other alto saxophone with the band.
And there was a piano player, Sammy Williams, and Othello Hepburn, he was on base and I played drums.
Boy, you got instant recall -- that's really great the way you remember those guys.
Oh, and we also had a guitar player,
his name was George Tucker.
And you guys played around at parties?

Oh, no; we had a big band, man. We played the ballrooms; we played all of the clubs -- that Hartley Toots wasn't able to play for, and they were able to get us cheaper anyway, so we got a lot of the gigs that Hartley Toots would have been playing. We played at the Elks, [Best.]
What was the going price for a night's gig then?
Well, I tell you. We used to share, like a dollar a man, and a dollar and a quarter for most.
That's about right.
Yeah, that's what we got for the gig.
Well, it was a start, though.

But we went on the road with this band when I was 14 years old, and a lot of people, they don't remember this, but there was a 16-cylinder Cadillac at one time with the running board on the side, and the two jump seats in the middle, so we carried 9 men in this one Cadillac -- no, ten! All in this one Cadillac; we had 10 men and in this one Cadillac. We had three in front, including the driver, we had three on the jump seat and then four on the back seat. We were very close, just like sardines.
Oh boy.
And this car used to run -- like every 60 miles we had to put oil in it.
That's what you'd call a close knit band.

Yeah. And then the bass drum and the bass violin rode on the top, and the trap rode on the running board, on the side of the running board, we had it enclosed where you could put the instruments and the suitcases and everything, and the ones who couldn't go on the outside, we held them in our laps -- and that's how we traveled.
Boy, what a picture. That's too much.

So then we finally worked up -- we were playing all these clubs around there; in fact, the band used to get like $50 a night for playing for this club, so what we would do, we would share like $1 apiece, and the rest of the money went into our Treasury to buy a bus -- so finally, we bought this bus which was a wreck before we got it. So we were going on the road -- at that time, I mean, we used to travel when school closed. Our school closed during the first week of June, so we would leave -- like school closed that Friday. Saturday, our first job would be at the Trianon Ballroom at Fort Lauderdale, which was a white dance we used to play.
Now this was a funny thing -- we used to -- we were
supposed to hit at nine o'clock, see. So we'd get on the bandstand at nine o'clock; now we couldn't leave that bandstand until 11:30 when it came time for intermission.

Now when intermission time came, we had to line up and they'd let all of the white men out of the toilet, and then we went in one by one and relieved ourselves and then got back on the bandstand and we sat there. And they would come up to the bandstand and say, "Hey, boy, do you know 'Sweet Georgia Brown?' and this kind of thing. "When are you niggers gonna get hot"?

So that's where we played; in fact, we were playing there all during the year, but when we got ready to leave on our tours, we would start out with Ft. Lauderdale on Saturday night, Sunday night we would play at the Sunset Auditorium in West Palm Beach -- that's where the Sunset Royals came from -- at West Palm Beach, we played Sunset Auditorium there, and that Monday night we were in Ft. Pierce, and then we just all worked our way up the coast all the way up to North Carolina.
Then we would cut across into Tennessee and come down through Mississippi.
My home town!
Yeah, and then back through Alabama and then to the west coast of Georgia, and then we'd come back down the west coast of Florida in time to be back home for school.
Hey, that's interesting.

Yeah, that's how we used to do that. But one time we were leaving Columbia, South Carolina, in this bus, and we got outside of Akens, and the motor fell out on the highway, so they had to pull us into Augusta, Georgia, and it cost $250 to get this bus fixed.

So what happened, we didn't want to send home and let our folks know that we were out there bad up, my first time getting stranded, and that's why up to this day I don't like cinnamon buns, because every time we got stranded, that's what I had to eat -- stale ones, at that!

So anyway, we got this bus fixed. Now we got the bus fixed, and -- oh, while we were waiting to get the bus fixed, we were stranded in Augusta for four days. Well, during those days, you could put up a sign and say it was a dance, and you had to play, like, the first half hour for free, and the people would come in and listen to the band, and if the band was good, they would come in -- they would let all the people out, and then they would charge admission for them to come in.
So they put a sign out that we were going to be playing the dance, while we were stranded there, and the old lady Crim, Miss Crim, that owned the hotel there in Augusta, Georgia ..
What town was this now?
In Augusta, Georgia. Miss Crim used

to take all the show people; everybody used to stay there at her place, but she was the one that let us stay in these rooms. We only had three rooms -- there were 12 of us then, but we had three rooms for 12 of us - and we had a girl vocalist, too, Sally Lou -- Sally was in there with us, but we had three rooms that she allowed us to have, and she told us, "Now when you all get the money, you send me back my money for the room."

So we stayed there, and we lived off stale cinnamon buns and water. That was our meal for the four days. So we played this dance, and we made enough money off this dance that we were able to pay for the bus, to get the bus out.

Now, we have to make our monthly payments on this bus, see, but with the bus breaking down and giving us all this trouble, we weren't able to make our payment. So we played in Athens, Georgia, for the university dance there. While we were playing the dance, the man from the bus company came up there and he said, "You hadn't made no payments in three months on this bus, and I want three months of payments or I'll take the bus from you."

Now, here we are -- stuck with no money, and we're playing the dance this night and hoping that we'll have a full house so we can pay the man for the bus. All right? Well, fortunately for us, we made the money to pay for the bus.
Now, we leave Athens, going in to Alabama into -- Millinder oh, where Lucky Miller was from in Alabama -- oh, where was that?
Not Birmingham, was it?

No, not Birmingham; not Doltham or none of those places. It was up north -- Andeston, Alabama, I think it was. But anyway, the promoter -- when we got in town, we got in touch with the promoter right away, and he stood good for us to eat, as we hadn't eaten all that day, see, so we got there that evening.

So I'll never forget this -- we got in there and the promoter made the arrangements for us to eat. So somebody came in there, where everybody was sitting down there with their heads down, they were sad and everything. Well, somebody came in and put -- at that time, it was 5¢ for the jukebox. They put -- there was 12 records on the jukebox then -- this was back in 1935, I think it was. Well, they put a nickel on one of Jimmy Luntzford's records, and I don't remember which one it was. I think it was For Dancers Only or something.

Well, anyway, they put this nickel on this record, and the record started playing and we all got up and started to dance, and the lady looked up at us and said, 'Lord, they sure was hungry' -- that was after we ate.
But while I was eating, I saw this black thing in my greens, and I didn't know what it was at first, but after
I took a closer look, it was a roach! So I politely picked this roach up and put him on the side, and kept on eating; man, I was so hungry -- I had never been so hungry in my life.

Oh, that's beautiful. You know, man, I'm so glad to hear you mention some of these things, because these experiences are so similar to most of us, and especially about these places where Miss Crim was.

Yeah, Miss Crim's hotel? Yeah. Well, it was an old man, too -- there was also a guy in Macon, Georgia, Mr. Douglas, he owned the Douglas Hotel there, and we got stranded again. We were in Macon, Georgia, and he allowed us to stay there, and we also ate -- he had a restaurant downstairs, and so we were able to also eat -- on Thanksgiving Day, I was eating me a 10¢ bowl of beef stew -- that was what we had.

And so -- do you know there was one thing about these people, you know, they saw that we were a bunch of young kids and they sympathized with us, you know, that we were struggling and trying to make it, so ...
(Interruption)
Go ahead and finish.

Well, you know, they knew we were out there struggling and trying to make it, and so they would allow us to owe them and you know, they would let us know -- 'You be sure and send me my money back', so when we had a good night, we would always remember, 'Hey, look,
we got to send x amount of dollars down to Miss so and so or Mr. so and so, because when we were stranded down there, we didn't pay them". You know what I mean?
So on many a night, instead of me drawing some money, the money went to pay bills, to buy gas or oil for the bus, and to send the money back to people that we owed. You know?
You know, that's quite a story. What ever happened to all of that honesty? People used to be so good about that, and the musicians really used to pay it back, too.
That's right. Yeah, they were very honest.
We had someone like that in New York -- Mr. Collins.

Yeah, old man Collins, sure. hey were good people, who really -- you know, you got stranded in these different cities and they would see that you ate and had a place to stay and they would always tell you, 'You know, when you get the money send it back to me' -- and they really used to send it back to these people.
And in all of these towns, there was somebody like this, in almost every city that you played in. You know, you remember the guy in Cincinnati? Uncle Henry?
Uncle Henry, yes.
And the woman in Atlanta, Georgia.
Mom Sutton!
Mom Sutton, yes.
And Mother Havelow in Philadelphia.
Yeah, in Philadelphia. I mean all of these towns had somebody like this, you know, who looked after the show people.

You know, you and I and guys like us have got to get together and sort of make a little memory of all these beautiful people all over the United States because it's a lost art -- people don't really know this, and I'm so happy to have you mention it here. The people who really helped us, because we had no hotels to stay in.
That's right.
And we stayed in these homes, and they were a good place to eat, in almost every town, and they really fed us the best they could.
That is right -- good wholesome food, too. I mean it wasn't the most expensive cuts of pork chops and stuff, but it was a good meal.
Yeah, the greens were good and the gravy and the rice -- you'd walk away filled.
Filled up, that's right.
This is beautiful--here we're sitting in Nice, France talking about
You know those little, lovely people out there who are in some small way responsible for us still being here today.
That's right.
Panama, this is beautiful. I've done quite a few of these things, and man, you're so literate with it, it's just a joy to sit here and listen to you like this.
Why thank you.
So let me tell you, anything else you want to say about your traveling days, go ahead.
Now here I was, you know, when I was coming up, I don't know whether I should say this or not -- if not, you can cut it out.
No -- if it's in your life, you say it, man.

Well, like me being the youngest one in the band, I was almost -- in fact, in all of the bands I played in, up until around World War II, I was the youngest one in the group or in the band, and one of the sayings was, the guy used to say to you, "You're not a man until you have a dose of gonorrhea."
Which was quite prevalent, too.

It was prevalent at that time. And you know, I heard the guys saying that, and I wanted to be a man, so here I am, at the age of 15, I got my first dose, and I walked up to this fellow who is here right now -- Ivan Rolay, and he'll tell you, because he used to take care of me; he was like my big brother in the band -- he used to give me hell all the time because I was always doing something dumb, you know?
He was the bass player with Jonah Jones.

Yeah, the bass player with Jonah Jones, Ivan Rolay. He used to give me hell all the time, but I ran up to him and I took it out and I showed it to him and I said, "I got it, I got it!" I was so proud, I said I was a man at last. And that next day, I was in tears -- I was in pain and everything else.
But that was my first experience of wanting to be a man, you know.
That's great, man.

So after that, I learned later on in life why these things happened to me, but you know, I was, like, I was sort of raised like a little girl in a way, because my mother never allowed me to -- like when I went out and worked, I couldn't spend any of my money like the other boys was able to, like George Kelly and those were able to get up the next morning and go and buy a pair of shoes or what not. During those days, you could put down, like a dollar on a suit and then pay $5 the next week, or something like that.

Well, me, I wasn't able to do anything like that; my mother took every nickel that I made, because I had to take care of her and my brother. See, and that's why I said earlier that I became a meal ticket, you know?
Uh huh.

So, anyway, when all of the other boys was able to have, like four and five suits of clothes, I had a suit, period, that I wore to church. And the rest of that money, my mother took it, and paid her bills with it and played the numbers, which I detest -- to this day, I don't play numbers to this day, because of that. And my mother would spend up all my money playing numbers.

But, anyway, I stayed with George Kelly's band until around 1938. I'll never forget -- I think it was May 2nd or something like that, in 1938, and Earl Hines played in Miami, and Hartley Toots was going to have a new drummer; they were going to have a change in drummers, so I went to Mr. Rivers who owned the band -- Bill Rivers owned the band, see. Because at that time, in the band, there was Cat Anderson in that band at that time, in 1938.
Which is here now.

Yeah, which is here now with us -- Cat Anderson was in the band. But I went to Bill Rivers, after the dance that night, because in Earl Hines' band, there was some great trumpet players at the time; Freddie Webster, Ray Nance, [Ed] McConnell, the trumpet -- and Pee Wee -- remember Pee Wee?
Yeah, I remember Pee Wee.
Because they were all the same height, remember? Both of them were short, but they could play.
Yeah, real short.

Well, anyway, I was at the dance that night, see, and I heard that Hartley Toots was looking for a drummer, so I went to Mr. Rivers, and I said to him you know, after the dance was over, he was walking -- because for some reason, I guess because I was young and I was a home grown boy, nobody around Miami thought I could play. But I thought I could play, I had a lot of confidence in myself that I could play.

So I went to Bill Rivers, and I asked him -- no, I didn't ask him, I had said to him, I said, "Look, Mr. Rivers, I heard that you were looking for a drummer. I would appreciate it if you would give me the opportunity to play in your band. I tell you what -- you don't have to pay me any salary for 2 weeks; just take care of my expenses, and if I prove myself all right, then you can put me on salary."

So Mr. Rivers, who was a tall man -- over 6 ft. tall -- he looked down at me and said, "Boy, who told you you could play the drums? Why don't you go home to your mother?" I cried all the way from Second Avenue and 9th Street to Fourth Avenue and 19th Street, I was in tears; I just couldn't believe that you know, I was willing to go in this band and work for nothing --
Just for a chance.
Yeah, just to give me a chance -- and
he said this to me.

So, it happened so George Kelly went to Tampa to join Andy [Gumm] and his band -- Andy [Gumm] Martin, he had a band, a 9 piece band over there. In Tampa. So there was another 9 piece band there, too, that was headed by Charlie Bradford ley. So they were looking for a drummer.

So I got a letter from George Kelly, because he had broken up our band that we had; he broke up the band, so he knew that I wasn't doing anything, so he wrote me a letter and told me that Charlie Bradford ley was looking for a drummer, so I wrote him a letter right away and told him, you know, that I would like to come up there and join the band.

So they sent for me. I went to Tampa, I'll never forget it -- I landed there on the 27th of May in Tampa, 1938, and I joined Charlie Bradford ley and the Florida Collegians -- that was the name of the band. So we used to play at the Frog's Rest, which was a club there, the Frog's Rest, on Friday night and the Cuban Club in Jabo City I on Saturday. And during the week, we had, like the social clubs, we probably had 2 or 3 of those jobs a week, like; maybe Monday, Wednesday or Tuesday and Wednesday. But we always played Friday and Saturday at the Frog's Club Rest and the Cuban Club.
So everything went along fine until around the latter part of July, and the work got slow. So I was laying in bed this Sunday, and I got the bright idea to write my father -- he

was in New York at the time, and I really didn't expect him to even send for me because I had been told so many bad things about him by my mother until I actually hated this man, and I used to write him some pretty nasty letters before I left Miami, that was dictated by my mother.

But, just for the hell of it, I said, 'Well, I'm gonna write to him and see if he'll send for me, you know, this no good cat.' That's how I felt. So I wrote him a letter and I told him that the people -- which was a lie -- that the people down here was talking about what a great drummer I was and that I should leave from down there and go to New York because I was just fooling around and wasting my time.

Now, none of this was true, but I just had this confidence in myself that I could play the drums, you know -- but me being a young kid, 18 years old at the time, I mean nobody paid any attention to me. So -- would you believe it -- he sent me a bus ticket as long as my arm, man; I'll never forget that. And sent me an extra five dollars.
This was 1938? What year was that?

This was 1938. And he sent me that extra $5. So I took the $5, at the time, my rent was $2.50 a week, so I took $2.50 of it, because like I said, we wasn't doing too much work, and the little bit of money I made I was trying to eat with, and the lady allowed me to stay there without paying any rent.
Uh huh.

And downstairs, where I lived at, there was a guy there who was in show business at one time -- called Kid Mason; he was a dancer, and he owned the candy store downstairs, and I used to go down there sometimes and he would feed me, you know?
What town was this at?
In Tampa, this is Tampa, Florida.
Uh huh.

So I went out and bought me a loaf of Marita bread, and a chicken, and I fried the chicken up Saturday, and made my box. And that Sunday morning, I left -- I think it was August 7th that I left Tampa, on a Sunday, on my way to New York.

Now, I got on this bus, in the back seat with my cardboard suitcase, and my drums. And I never got off that bus but once, and that was in Augusta, Georgia; I went to the bathroom there. The whole time, I stayed on that bus, which took 2 days and 2 nights to get from Tampa to New York.

Now when we got to Richmond, Virginia, and I didn't see any front porches, I was shocked; I said, 'These people don't have any front porch!' You know, they had the steps and you walked right into the house, and as we got up to Washington, it just got worse. My imagination was just -- you know, they don't have no front porch, because I was so used to seeing front porches down south, see.
So I got to New York that morning about six o'clock, and my father was there to meet me. At that time, the Greyhound bus terminal was at 50th Street, do you remember?
Right.
Yeah, 50th Street between Broadway and 8th Avenue. That's where my father met me.
Yeah, you know, I had forgotten that.

And I got off the bus and he was standing there, and at first, I didn't recognize him because I hadn't seen him since I was 11 years old, and now I'm 18 going on 19, you know, and it looked like him, but I wasn't sure -- and I said, 'Yeah, that's him!' -- because he was smiling and everything.

So when I got off the bus, I walked down the steps and he was there to greet me and he hugged me and he went to kiss me, and I turned my head, because I didn't want him kissing me, because you know, like I said, all these things that had been told to me by my mother, and I really used him -- that's what I did -- so I could get to New York.

So anyway, that's how I was able to come to New York. Now, the first night I'm in town, I go out jamming. I went by Jocks, I went by the Rennie, I went to the 721 Club up there on St. Nicholas Avenue, that's where I first saw Jabbo Smith. He was playing there.
Where was that? The Rennie?
Yeah, the Rennie -- the Renaissance, and Jocks, and the 721 Club -- that was at 146th Street and St. Nicholas Avenue. That was where I first saw Jabbo Smith, who was playing there.
Yeah ...
And I asked if I could sit in, and they looked at me, because at that time, I only weighed 121 lbs; I was the littlest guy, and I looked like I was about 14 years old.

So they asked me how old I was, so I told them I was 18, but I said I'd be 19 in December --and this was August. So they said, "And you can play?" -- and I said, "I think so." So I got up on the bandstand and I started playing, and everybody started looking around at me, and I played the same thing when I went to Jocks and the same at the Rennie.
So I went -- there was a club on 116th Street called the Masopeka, and I went there; that was where I first heard Lips Page and Roy Eldridge; they had a jam session there, and I sat in there.

So it happened there was a saxophone player was also there by the name of Tab Smith. Tab Smith heard me, and so he asked me if I was working with some band around town, and I said, "No, I'm not -- I just came here from Florida" -- and I had a southern accent you could cut with a knife at that time, and so he said, "Well, how long have you been in town?"

And I said, 'Well, I just got here -- I only been here like 2 days.' So he said, 'Would you like to join my group?', so I told him yes, and he said, 'Well, can you start with me Sunday night?' I said, 'Yeah' -- and I didn't ask how much the job paid or nothing.

So he asked me if I belonged to the union and I told him no, and he said, 'Well, that's all right, because at this club, it's non-union anyway'. At that time, the union was still trying to get clubs to join, so this was a non-union club, the Rosebud, which was run by the uncle of Thelma Carpenter. I remembered Thelma when she was like 11 or 12 years old -- yeah, her uncle owned this club, the Rosebud, it was on Franklin and Carson; or I mean, on Fulton and Carson Avenue in Brooklyn.
Oh, in Brooklyn.
Yeah. So after only being in New York 5 days, I went to work at the Rosebud.
The first night you were in town, you really met some giants -- you met Jabbo Smith, this was the trumpet player of that era, along with the great Louis Armstrong.
Right.
He was really great, and you met the great Tab ...
Tab Smith.
Tab Smith, who was one of the giant alto players of the time.
And Lips Page.
Lips Page, right.
And Roy.
Roy Eldridge, yeah -- so you really fit in good company there. I just want to make a note of that so people will know who those guys were at that time.

And then, like the third night, that was the first time I ran in to Cozy Cole. There was a club at 142nd Street, and 7th Avenue -- oh my God, I can't remember, right down the street from the Woodside Hotel. The guy that had the group, and it was Freddie Moore; Freddie Moore, the drummer. Freddie Moore had the group in there --
And what was this club?
142nd Street and 7th Avenue, right on the corner.
Gee, I can't recall it either.

Yeah, well, anyway, that's the first time I ran in to Cozy Cole. Cozy Cole, Charlie Christian and [Fred Rand] was in town, and a guitar player that was with him that first started the multiple sounds on the recording --
Oh yeah ...
Yeah, his name was Les Paul, remember him?
Right. Sure.
Yeah, that was the first time I heard him and Charlie Christian; they hooked up together that night, because I played the drums behind them.
So that was my first time running into Cozy Cole, too. Man, I was looking at this cat with my mouth open, I had heard so much about Cozy Cole when I was in Florida.
Right. Well, Cozy Cole and I were working together with Cab Calloway at that time.
No kidding?

Yeah, 1938. He had taken Leroy Maxey's place, because we came downtown in 1936 when the Cotton Club opened down on Broadway, and we opened with Leroy Maxey playing drums. And that's the same time that Benny Goodman opened at the Pennsylvania Hotel with Lionel Hampton and Teddy Wilson and the Quartet.
Oh, yeah.

And we used to meet on our intermissions and hang out together on 52nd Street, and Gene Krupa was beginning to play those drum solos, and Cab Calloway heard Gene Krupa play, and he wanted a drum soloist. Well, poor Maxey had never encountered that -- playing drum solos; he was a great show drummer for the shows, but he didn't know nothing about doing solos, and that's when Cab was looking for somebody that could do a Gene Krupa number.
Yeah, Gene Krupa.
And that's how Cozy came in.
Well, I'll be darn.
So it all ties in there.

Yeah, I first met Cozy Cole -- up there and my eyes popped wide open; I didn't know about the Rhythm Club yet. See, this was about my third night in town. Well, the next day, I heard that -- that night, I heard them talking about the Rhythm Club. Well, I had heard the guys down in Miami talk about the Rhythm Club, too; that's where all the musicians used to hang out, see.
Right, right.

So I only lived at 131st Street at Lenox Avenue at the time, with my father. So I went by the Rhythm Club the next day, and the next guy I saw, he was in Miami with his band then at one time, and I saw him, and I introduced myself to him -- this was Kaiser Marshall. He was sharp, boy; you know, he was a sharp dresser, anyway, you know. And I met Kaiser Marshall, and I reminded him of who I was, because you know, I saw him down in Miami when he came to play at the Delorobia.

So I went to the Rhythm Club and I met another guy that I'd heard about, but I didn't know him, and he was from Miami -- that was Cedric Wallace, he was playing with Fats Waller, and I met him, and I met -- oh, quite a few guys, like Cookie Mason, who was also from Florida; I think he was
from St. Augustine, Florida, a trumpet player -- all these different guys I met, and I was just standing there with my mouth open, I says, "Here I am, in New York and all these great musicians!"
And you know, getting ready to go to work that Sunday night on my first job, I tell you ...
Where was that job going to be at?
At the Rosebud. With Tab.
Oh yeah.

And here it is, the people down there in Miami told me that I couldn't play, so what happened -- while I'm working at the Rosebud, the news gets back to Miami that I'm playing with a group -- only been in New York a week, and they hear I'm working. I get this long letter, which I still have in my scrapbook, from Bill Rivers.
Oh no! " Get away, boy."

Yeah -- and telling me that he had heard about what happened to me in New York and he would like me to join Hartley Toots band and they were getting ready to go on the road -- and you know, I didn't even answer that letter; I never did answer that letter. But I have it in my scrapbook because that is one of my fond memories of him breaking my heart that Sunday night.
You know, I've done a lot of these, as I said before, and you're the first guy that mentioned anything
about Kaiser Marshall, and I'm so happy, because I knew him, and he was a great band drummer at that time -- and he was from Texas; from Texas, if I remember correctly.
No, he's from Augusta, Georgia. He was a Georgia boy. Yeah, his mother lived in Texas, but he was from Augusta, Georgia; that's where Kaiser was from.
Yeah, and we all know about Zooty and Sid, but nobody seems to mention Kaiser.
He was a great ...
He was a great cymbal man.
Great cymbal; in fact, the story was that he was the guy that invented the high hat cymbal.
Probably so, because he had that triple thing that he played on those cymbals.
That's right. Yeah. And a great dresser, too, man.
Oh, great dresser.

Well you know, to have the opportunity at that age, you know, young -- a young guy to be seeing all these great musicians that I had been hearing about, and here I am, you know, rubbing shoulders with them and standing and talking to them, and at that time, I used to stutter worse than I do now, and I couldn't say two words, I was just so carried away with meeting these people, man. It was really a great experience for me.
Oh yeah.
I'm gonna tell you a funny story. After working at the Rosebud for about 3 weeks, the union representative -- I don't know if you remember him -- Redman.
Sure, sure.

Well, he came by then and he threatened Walter, who was the owner of the club; he threatened Walter, that he was going to have some signs put out front and pickets walking in front of the place if the club didn't go union.

Now, we got to join the union. Well, I think the piano player and myself was the only two that wasn't union, but the rest of the guys were union, and they were working a non union gig, and Redman couldn't say anything to them about it, you know?
Yeah.

But he wanted the place to become union. Now, my father -- I was still at home living with him now -- I went home and I told him, I said, 'Well, look daddy, I'm gonna lose my job if I don't join the union' -- so he say, 'How much it cost?' So I told him it cost $54; you remember that at that time, it was $50 to join and $4 for your first 3 months dues. So I told him it was $54.

Well, at that time, my father was working on the WPA, but he was working during the days. I don't know, but he was always pretty smart in his way; I learned later on that he was no dummy. So he went to the foreman with this

sad story and told him that his son had just come from Miami, and was playing in the band and the place he was playing in, he was gonna lose his job because he doesn't belong to the union, and he just had to join the union, and he didn't have the money for him to join the union, but he has insurance that he belonged to that would pay him $25 a week if he got sick.

So would he let him work at night and he would give him -- a little taste if he we would change the schedule and let him work at night for a month so he could get this money together to put me in the union, because he was going to the pawn shop to pawn some suits if he wasn't able to get this money to put me in the union.

So this foreman, I guess, felt sorry for him, and he put him on at night, so what my father would do is, you know, it's hard for them to tell whether there is anything wrong with your head or your back, you know ...
Right.
So if he hurt his back on the job, you'd never know. So he laid up there all day, and collected $25 a week, and that's how I got in the union!
That's a beautiful story, man.

Yeah, that's how I joined Local 802, but he had -- that's why he had to do it for a month, because he had to pay the foreman off, you know, give him some a taste for switching him, and letting him work at night, and also have enough money to take care of his expenses, and the $54 to put
me in the union -- and it took a month to do it. So that's how we did it, and that's how I joined Local 802.
That's wild, really.
So, right after that, there was a guy that had a six piece group named Billy Hicks, that was called Billy Hicks and his Sizzler Six.
I remember him.
Trumpet player.
Yeah, that's right.

Yeah. Well, he was looking for a drummer, and I joined him. And I was playing a whole lot of different hotels then, and at that time, they were still using black groups in different rooms of the different hotels, the St. Regis and all those hotels around New York. So I was playing with him, like we'd probably play 2 nights at the St. Regis, we played one night at the Astor, you know, and two nights at the Waldorf. But that's how we worked.

So, now, this is around about -- November, it's around November, so about the first of the year, I'm getting the chance to go in to the Apollo Theatre with Billy Hicks. But we got to play show. Now I can't read no music, see. I still can't read, you know.
Uh huh.
But we're gonna play this show. I'll never forget this guy Henry Wessell; he had just come back from
Europe.
Trumpet player?

No, he was an actor. I think his name was Wessell -- Henry Wessell; I'm not sure. But anyway, at that time, at the Apollo Theatre, all the shows had like a story behind it, you know? Like 'A Night in Spain,' and all the music was Spanish music, you know? That type thing.
Yeah.

So now here I am, getting ready to play my first show, and I was playing the jive shows in the nightclub where the singer would get up and sing two choruses of 'Dinah' or something and go around the table. But for a [real big] production, I ain't never played anything like that.

So I'll never forget this man as long as I live -- Tom Whaley. Tom Whaley was the conductor for the first show; then after that, Henri Woode would take over, but the first show was conducted by Tom Whaley.
He was the musical director.

Yeah, he was the musical director there. So now, we're at rehearsal and I can't read nothing, but I'm listening. And every time they would start out a number, I would drop a stick or something, and I'd be trying to find the stick while I'm listening to what the band was playing. Listening to what the band was doing, and then when
they ran over it again, I would start playing. And I'd be playing it -- and I'd be playing it right; I didn't know what I was doing, but whatever I did, it was right; it was acceptable.

Now, we're getting ready to play the first show, this Friday morning -- I'm scared to death. So I went to Tom and I said, "Mr. Whaley, I've never played a show before in my life, and I don't know how to play this show; I don't know what to do." And he turned to me and said, "You mean to tell me you were downstairs yesterday and you were playing and you don't ..." And I said, "I can't read anything." And he said, "Oh my God. Well, I tell you what you do. Keep your foot off that bass drum, don't play that bass drum until you know where the tempo is, and there is always somebody who has the lead, and you watch my stick and listen for the lead and you'll come out all right."

And I never forgot that; that's the reason I could play a show and didn't even have to have any music if I have somebody up front that could give me the right downbeat and everything; I have no problems at all, playing the show. But that's how I learned how to play a show; Tom Whaley taught me.
That's beautiful.
How to play a Yeah, for his show. 1939.
Yeah, if you can just get that time from the conductor, the beat -- that's a clever thing.
Yes sir. That's how I learned to play shows; Tom Whaley taught me; he said, 'Keep that foot off that base drum, Charlie! Until you know where the tempo is.
Right.
So I played my first show at the Apollo around the month of January of 1939.

I think right here we ought to say in the tape who Tom Whaley is; he was one of the great writers and copyists and accompanists and arrangers, extracting all the scores of Duke Ellington, down through the years and was Duke's best friend until he died. And one of the saddest things -- I don't know if you ever knew this, but one of the saddest things was that Tom knew exactly how Duke wrote -- any little scrap of newspaper, or any scrap of paper that Duke put anything down on, Tom would know just how to orchestrate it.
That's what I was told.

Yeah, he would know exactly how to orchestrate it. And the only person that ever learned to do that was a bass player, a friend of yours and mine -- a young bass player, named Joe Benjamin, which Tom taught.
That's right -- he was his protege.
That's right. I remember. Yeah.

And the most sad thing about this whole thing is that Joe Benjamin died, and Duke died and Tom Whaley has gone blind; he's completely blind, so there is nobody that really knows exactly what all those masses of scores that Duke left;
there is nobody who really knows how to extract them, like Tom Whaley and Joe Benjamin.
I'll be darned.
So it's a very sad thing. And we knew Tom, because he was the guy at the Apollo, as Panama said.
He was something else, man. I think he finished at the Boston Conservatory and he was really a well rounded musician.
Yeah, same category as Eubie Blake.
Yeah. He's like Eubie; the same type of man. Same type of guy.
Yeah, same type. And I think he's still with us, but he's blind. I think he lives at the Henderson Hotel; I've had him over to my house since he's been blind and talked to him on tape.
I'll try to look him up, because he's a man that started -- that taught me how to play a show, and I feel obligated to him, I really do.
Well, the Ellington family still takes care of him and he's got a room there at the Henderson Hotel.
The Henderson Hotel at 50th and Seventh Avenue?
Yeah, Seventh Avenue.
No kidding, I'll go by and ask for him, when I go back to New York.
Yeah, do that, man.
I didn't know he was blind or anything like that.
Well, it was just so nice to hear you mention it, because so many of these things, this is so much about history, and your recitation is really going to be something.

So, I stayed with Billy Hicks until around the latter part of May, I think it was, and I was in a jam session; you know, because during those days, I mean, every place -- the places to jam were all over, and that's why the unions stopped jamming, because the nightclub operators used to hire like a piano and a drummer, and they'd start at nine o'clock, and nine thirty, you had a whole band up on the stage for free. So that's why the unions stopped jam sessions.
