I feel in a way, that I was partly responsible for some of the things that happened, because like I said in the beginning before I joined Cab Calloway's band, that I was a pretty wild little guy; I wasn't a big drinker and I couldn't smoke pot because -- marijuana -- because it put me to sleep -- when everyone else was getting high and feeling good, I went to sleep, so I could never smoke it.
And Cab didn't allow it in his band.

Right, Cab didn't allow it in his band, anyhow, and I wasn't a big drinker, because I could suffer with a hangover worse than anybody you ever saw. So my weakness was the girls. Yeah, I loved the girls, you know? So this was one of the problems that Helen had with me in the early part of our marriage.
Uh huh.

But like I said, after I joined Cab's band, I really cooled down to the stage where there was nobody else but her, although at the time, it was too late -- I think the horse was out of the barn, because she didn't believe it.
Well, that's unfortunate that that happened. Hey, what was your first car, man?

My first car -- and this is a funny story -- I did a recording date at Fulton Studio, that was the name of it at the time, at 40th Street and 6th Avenue. And I think, if I'm not mistaken, it was a date that I did with Joe Turner when I recorded "Corina Corina" with him. So I come downstairs, and it's beginning to rain, slightly. After awhile, it started coming down a little heavy, and I'm waving for the cabs, because at that time, I didn't have any wheels on my drum case or nothing, and the studio - they didn't start using bass drums or tom toms in the studio yet, so ...
Had to bring your own stuff?

You had to bring your own drums. So here I am standing on 6th Avenue, 40th Street, trying to get a cab, and they're passing me by like I wasn't there. So I got another date starting at 7 o'clock at Capital, which was like 6 -- almost 7 blocks away, and I got all these drums tocarry, and it's raining.

So I stood there and stood there, waving and waving, and I'm getting wet and the rain is getting harder, so I finally decided that I better do something -- so I took my bass drum, put it under my arm, and I took my tom toms and put that over my arm and with the drum case, and I picked it all up -- I don't know where I got the strength from -- but I picked all of this stuff up and walked from 40th Street to 46th Street, near Broadway to Capital Studio -- soaking wet.

I'm cursing, I'm mad; you could fry an egg on my head I was so mad, and I'm cursing the cab drivers and everything else, and I said, 'I'm gonna buy me a car.' So the next morning, the next day I didn't have a recording session until that night, so I came downstairs and I saw one of my neighbors, Jack Brown. And I said to Jack, I said, 'Hey, Jack, do you know anything about cars?' He said, 'A little bit', and I said, 'Well, look, I want to buy a car, and I just looked in the paper here and I see they got a 1953 Ford out here at the Ford Company out here in Flushing -- do you have time to go out there with me and look at it and see if
it's all right?" So he says, "Yeah, I'll go with you; I got nothing to do -- I'm off today."

So Jack and I got on the subway and we went out to Long Island and I saw the car, and he looked at it and inspected it, and I didn't know how to drive, because all those years I had either been in cars with the band or in a bus -- I never had to drive a car in my life.

But I was determined. We got the car, I think I paid $900 for it. This was 1954, but it was a '53 car, a Ford. And so Jack is driving it home, and we came across the 59th Street Bridge, so we had to go through Central Park, so we get to Central Park, and during those days when I was riding in the busses, I used to ride, like, up front, and where the door was, like, if I wasn't sleepy, I would go there and watch the bus driver and see the way he shifted gears and stopped the bus and everything.
Uh huh.

So I had an idea of how it was supposed to go. So when we got by the middle of Central Park, I said to Jack, I said, "Jack, I'm gonna take it home from here." I was scared to death, but like I said, I was determined. I got behind the wheel and I drove the car home. Now I can't park it. So he had to park it for me. This was around about one o'clock that day.
So, I knew I had to go and get me a learner's permit.
Yeah.

So I rush downtown to the motor vehicle bureau, and I told the lady that I'd like to get a learner's permit. So she said, "You know what? We just got a cancellation here. Do you think you would be ready in, say, 10 days?" I said, "Yes, ma'am".

Now I had never driven a car before in my life, now, but I told her, "Yes ma'am" and I guess the man upstairs must have been smiling on me because He made it possible for this cancellation to happen, because I never heard of this happening before, anyway.

So anyway, I get the learner's permit, rush back uptown, I saw one of my neighbors sitting out there, Walter, and I said to Walter, "What you doing?" and he said, "I ain't doing nothing" so I said, "Well, look, I need someone to sit with me in the car -- for my learner's permit, and would you ride along with me? I'll buy you a bottle", because he liked to drink anyway, so I said I'd buy him a bottle, and he said, "Yeah, I will go -- you don't have to buy me no bottle" -- and I said, "Oh, I'll buy you a bottle anyway, after we finish."

So he got in the car with me, and I started out, and one of the things that I heard that was very hard to do was learn to park. So every open space I saw, I sat up there trying to park this car. I tried to park this car, and he would get out and show me ... so that night, I got -- while I was down at the motor vehicle bureau, I got a pamphlet on

driving, and it showed you how the car, how you back the car up and when you get to where the door is, you start cutting in and everything, and I figured the thing out in my mind. Do you know on that 10th day, which was on a Friday, I went and took my test, and that Monday I had my driver's license, and I been driving ever since.
That's beautiful.
They left me out in the rain like that!
That's beautiful, man. That was 1954 -- this is 1978, and I'm not driving yet.
Well, if you had gotten wet like I did, you probably would have made up your mind then to drive.

But for a musician, it's very important, very monumental -- that first car, especially for a rhythm section man, a drummer, that's one of the reasons I really wanted to ask that question. But there's a lot of things in the fifties here which I wanted to parallel with your family, and where did you go from there when you and Helen split up? What did you do then with your life?

Well, I tell you -- my life was awfully rough. I was involved -- I was fortunate enough that I was involved with a psychiatric social worker -- her name was Iris, and her brother was a great jazz Dixieland jazz fan, band-player, back then.
So I was working on the weekend at the Central Plaza, which was a place where all the musicians used to work on Friday and Saturday.
Right, a good gig, huh?
Yeah, it was a good gig. I was a house drummer there for 10 years, see.
Beautiful.

So he used to come, like, once a month on business -- his name was Don Zenn, he owned an acoustical business, so he used to come to New York once a month and whenever he came up to Central Plaza, he would buy a bottle and the guys would go and sit at his table, and drink.
Well, like I say, I never was a big drinker anyway, so I would take like one drink with the rest of the guys and they'd be sitting there drinking him under the table.
So he took a liking to me, and he also said that I was a pretty honest guy, that he liked the way I talked when he and I would discuss things, so we became good friends.

So this night, he brought his sister along, and introduced her to me, and as fate would have it, she was just coming out of psychiatric school, from Columbia University, because she and her husband had divorced and she had gone back to school. She got her Master's degree as a social psychiatric worker.
So when I came off the bandstand, and he introduced

me to her, I sat there and I had a drink -- and I didn't have too much to say. So I went back on the bandstand, but when I came off again, she said to me, "You know? I been looking at you and you sitting up there and think you're smiling, and you're sitting there with a frown on your face -- you're not smiling. Who you kidding?"

So with her talking to me that way, I became very indignant and I asked her how did she know that I was sitting up there with a frown on my face, and she said, "Because this is gonna be part of my work when I get my degree, when I graduate." I said, "What kind of work you gonna do?" and she said, "I'm gonna be a psychiatric social worker".

And she said to me, she said, "Why don't you come by my house and sit and talk with me?" Well, I didn't pay any attention to it, I told her okay, but I went back on the bandstand, and I forgot about it.
Well, I was -- at the time, I was living in a room that was as big as a matchbox.
What was her name again? Iris ...
Iris Lewin. Iris Lewin was her name.
Oh, uh huh.
So I was sitting in the room one day, and I called Helen --
Your wife, Helen?

My wife Helen, yes, and I was really hurting and I really wanted to go back home -- in fact, I left home because of the violence that was going on, I just got tired of it because I don't consider myself a violent person, but I had to be in self defense.
So one morning, I had recorded all day -- I did 4 record dates that day, starting out at ten o'clock that morning, I didn't finish until three the following morning.

And I'm coming home, and as I turned the corner, I saw the light on in the living room and I knew what to expect when I saw the light on. But with all due respect to her, she had a problem with the bottle. And whenever I saw the light on, I knew that she was sitting there drunk, waiting on me. And the first thing she said to me was: 'What woman were you out with?' and I told her, I said, 'Well, look, you've got my schedule there, you know that I been working all day; for Christ's sake, why don't you go to bed?' and one word led to another, and we got into this violence again, which I deplored.

So I decided to just pack up some clothes and go away from home for a week or so, and by me going away probably, it would bring her back to her senses, and everything would be all right, not knowing that this was what she was hoping I would do, because I was never able to go back home after that.
In other words, this thing backfired on me,

and I guess that's why it hurt me so bad, because I thought that we were able to make up, that she was going to miss me, and was gonna come and get me -- because I went to the YMCA, I didn't even go to a hotel where I could have some other woman or something to come up there and comfort me -- but I went to the YMCA.
So when I got ready to go back home, she had changed all the locks on the door, and that was the thing that started me on my way down.
So anyway, you got to meet Iris after that.

Yeah. Well, I cried for three years on her shoulder; I cried -- I could be sitting down just holding a conversation, and I would just bust out in tears. That's one of the things she'd say that was a good thing for me, that I was able to cry, because if I had kept it all in, I probably would have fallen apart -- but by me being able to cry, I was able to get these feelings out of me.

And so later on, we sort of fell in love with each other, and we got married. At the time I got married to her, I was Dinah Shore's personal drummer, and Dinah, who is one of the finest human beings I ever met in my life, I really regret that I left her, because I couldn't have worked with anybody better than her -- and when I got ready to leave, when I got ready to get married, Dinah asked me, she said, "What are you getting married for again, Panama?
After all you've been through, you're gonna get right back into something like that again?" And I said, "Well, Dinah, she loves me and I love her, and I want to get married" and so we got married.
Yeah, we'll get back to Dinah -- I want to get to her and some of the differnt bands you played with during this era, so let's leave that for awhile. But you did marry Iris, then?
Yeah.
Do you know what year that was?
Yeah, I married Iris in 1970.

1970. I just want to bring this all into perspective with what we ... I just want to bring everything into perspective, the family, and personal side of your family life, in perspective with what you were doing musically.

So if we could skip back now for a minute with the music, we've been through the Cab Calloway scene. Now comes the fifties and the sixties, where the recording thing started, and that was a great era for you, because without a doubt, you were probably one of the most recorded drummers during the fifties and sixties, I dare say -- you had quite a career. How did you get into that, Panama?
Well, Leroy Kirkland Curtlin lived in the same building that I lived in.
He was an arranger and a guitarist?
Right. Leroy Kirkland. He used to play with the Sunset Royals.
Uh huh.
And he started doing the rock and roll dates for record companies around New York, and at first, the first rock and roll record was really made by Joe Marshall.
Yeah, that's what I wanted to ask you -- I had his name down here, I wanted to ask you about Joe Marshall.

Joe Marshall made the first rock and roll record with Ruth Brown and Lavern Baker and these people, and then I think he recommended me to Leroy Kirkland, because Leroy Kirkland told me that he was using Joe Marshall on these dates.
Joe Marshall got to be the drummer with Arthur Godfrey.

Yeah, that's how I got it. Now this is a funny story, too, because when that happened, he and I met -- it was on a Christmas, and Joe had just left Arthur Godfrey, and I was hitting and missing, and we were both -- I was crying on his shoulder, and there's a funny thing about Joe -- he doesn't cry. He said, 'Man, everything is gonna be all right' -- just like we were in the Braddock Bar, and we ...
That's on 126th Street, right?
On 126th Street and 8th Avenue where we were splitting a beer -- that's how poor we were.
So you were all drining at the Braddock Bar at 126th and 8th Avenue?
Eight Avenue. And I was crying on his shoulder and he was crying on my shoulder, because he had just left Arthur Godfrey and I was hitting and missing.

I had just left Duke, and I had come back to New York, and there wasn't that much happening, and he told me, he said, "Well, Panama, everything is gonna be all right" -- and so he was recording, he started recording with Atlantic Records with Jesse Stone and Leroy Kirkland.
Uh huh.

And I think this date came up where he couldn't make it and he recommended me to Leroy Kirkland, and so Leroy Kirkland was living in the same building that I was living in, on the same floor, and he rang the bell and asked me if I could make a record date.

Well, I had made no recordings on the outside, other than recording with the bands that I was with, and so I told him yes. Well, I didn't know what kind of music we were supposed to play, but I did have experience as a little boy, when I was around about 10 years old, I used to play at the Church of God on Sundays -- that was my gig, see.
So I knew how to play spiritual and gospel music,

I knew the rhythms for it. So when I got on the date, that's what we were doing -- we were doing like rhythm and blues -- that was before it got labeled rock and roll-- we were doing rhythm and blues.
Right.
And so I recorded with Laverné Baker, I think that was the first rock and roll date that I did, was with her. But Joe Marshall was partly responsible for me doing that.

Let's see if you and I can historically bring this thing, which is most important -- and your memory is much better than mine. But when we worked together, you came into Cab Callaway's band in 1946, and I had come in at 1936, so I had been in the band 10 years when you came in.
So then we worked together from 1946 to 1951, we worked together, right?
Yeah.
We went to South America; one of the last big trips was down to Montévideo, South America, with Cab -- that was about '51, I think.
In 1951, because I took a band down there -- for some reason, in South America, which is a rhythmic country --- all those countries are rhythmic down there, and so the drummer is the star.
You were a star there.
I was a star down there, and so I

got a chance to take a band back there in 1954. I took a six piece band down there, and we were supposed to be like the relief band for the Spanish band, Nora Morales -- they were the featured band and we were like the relief band.
Uh huh.

And they were playing on the inside of the theatrical celise, and we were playing outside. And they had to play the show, and they would -- all the people that paid all this money to be in there with their tuxedos and everything on -- and we were outside for the low lifes, the people that weren't able to afford the tuxedos and things.
The festival folks.
The festival folks, right. But we were such a sensation down there, that after about 4 nights, we became the featured band and Nora Morales was the fill-in band.

That's great. Well, that's the reason I wanted to tie that in, because we had been down there in '51, and we really had a ball -- it was a beautiful thing, that country, and I remember how well you were a star -- they just loved you down there, and see, the reason why they had you to come back in '54.
So then you come back to the States in '54, and that's when you really get into this recording business.
Oh, I really got into the recording business then.
And you got in with Joe Marshall and Leroy Kirkland.
And then Jesse Stones was in there.
Right, and then I remember where you got to do demo records with Clyde Otis.
Clyde Otis, right.

And then you got me in on that gig, and I remember you brought me in on the Clyde Otis thing with Bedford Hendrix who made the arrangements, and we got to be like a demonstration group for Clyde Otis, and Clyde went to Mercury, and we were really in, and you being the drummer, you were the guy who was in -- I remember you really brought me into that.
So you go and tell about that whole era now. With that Clyde Otis era, the fifties, and it was Mercury records.
Well, I think I have to go back a little bit before that.
Okay, good.
You see, they just made a movie the other day called The Buddy Holly Story.
Oh, I heard about that.

"The Buddy Holly Story," which everybody is raving about it. But nobody knows that he was recording down south or wherever he was, but his first big record, "Peggy Sue", was recorded in New York City and Dick Jacobs
was the A&R man, and I was the drummer on that.
That was for Decca, then?
For Decca, right. We had made "Peggy Sue" and nobody ever, you know, they made this movie and nobody ever said anything about that.
His first hit.

Yeah, that was his first hit. You know, like with Elvis Presley -- I'm goin' in that area now. Now, Elvis Presley -- there was a guy named Otis Blackwell -- he wrote "Don't Be Cruel" for Presley and "All Shook Up" -- these were all written by Otis Blackwell.
Right, I know him very well.

Otis Blackwell -- we used to make (Interruption) demonstration records that he used to send down to Nashville for Presley to learn. And if you listen to these demonstration records and listen to Presley, you will hear Otis Blackwell, because he sang "Don't Be Cruel" and "All Shook Up" exactly like Otis Blackwell sang them -- note for note.
Beautiful.
And we used to make quite a few demos for the [Hillary Range] Publishing Company that they used to send down there to Nashville and Memphis for Elvis Presley to learn.
And I remember Bobby Darin -- I did Bobby Darin's first big hit record, "Splish Splash". And after the record

became a big hit, that's when he did the album that they used the all white band on, and I met him a couple of days afterwards, and said to him, I said, "Look, Bobby, man, why didn't you call me to do your date?" and he said to me, "Well, you know, when you move up in the world, you change company", and that was his answer to me for not using me on this date.

Then, I recorded, like all of the Platters records. I made "The Great Pretender", "Stardust", oh, let's see, "The Great Pretender", "Stardust", "Harbor Lights" -- in fact, everything that the Platters made with Tony Williams, I was playing drums on.
Uh huh.

Then I made "Tweedlie Dee" and "Jim Dandy" with Lavern&Baker. I did all of Brook Benton's -- "Endlessly", "Just a Matter of Time", "Kitty O". With Dinah Washington, I did "What A Difference a Day Makes" which was a big hit record, and also with Brook Benton, I recorded "Fools Rush In".
I was in on many of those, too.
You were on many of those records, right; you were playing base on them with me.
Sure.
And also, I did "Fever" with Little Willie John, where later on, the tune was recorded by Peggy Lee and became a big classic. I did, "Drown in My Own Tears"

"Hallelujah, with Ray Charles, and "Hallelujah, I Love Her So" with Ray Charles and "Maryann". I also did the only million selling record that Sarah Vaughn ever had, I was playing drums on, called "Haunting Melody". I was playing drums on that.
Wow.

I also recorded "Earth Angel" with a group called the Penguins, which was a big hit. I did "Summer Winds" with Wayne Newton; I recorded a song that -- now here's a story for you -- I did the "Colonel Bogie's March" with Mitch Miller, which was a big hit. They wanted a field drum sound -- I was always figuring out sounds and things, and so they wanted a field drum sound, but they didn't have a field drum there, and I don't know where I got the idea from, but it dawned on me, and I said to Jimmy Carroll, who was an arranger, I said, "Jimmy, how do you think it would sound if I put my snare drum on the top of this timpani?" -- which was a 25 inch timpani -- and I put the snare drum on top of the timpanny, and we started playing, and it sounded just like a field drum, and that's how we got that field drum sound on "Colonel Bogie's March".

Then I did another record that sold almost two million records -- that was Perez Prado, a tune called "Patricia". That was another thing where they had these tapes that were recorded out in California, and the A&R man, who was Herman Diaz, was on the verge of losing his job, and so

he was trying to do something to save his job, and he got this guitar player, Billy Muir, to -- in fact, that was one of the first times that I knew of that they did a thing called overdubbing, and it was the first time I ever heard a base guitar on a recording. It was Billy Muir, Alan Hannon and myself.

Billy Muir had written out some parts for me to play and for himself to play, and Alan to play -- and we were trying to overdub to these tapes that Perez Parado had done out in California - and one of the tunes was "Patricia" that we were trying to do.

So we were getting ready to call the date off because it wasn't making it, and Herman was a little let down and everything, and I got the bright idea -- I said, "Hey Herman, look, why don't you try this. Let Alan Hannon play what he's playing on the base guitar, let Billy Muir play this rhythm on the tambourine" -- and I played the rhythm for him that I wanted him to play on the tambourine, which I still have that tambourine -- I saved that tambourine. "And I'll play straight eights with a backbeat on the drum with brushes and let's see how it sounds" -- so he said, "Okay, we'll try it."
So they ran the tape, and we played 8 bars -- and Herman said, "Let's make it" and it became a hit for Perez Parado and it saved his job, too.
Beautiful!

So then what happens, though, I did an album with him after that, one of the tunes was in it was "Why Wait?" which was a big hit again, but I made this album and it changed contracts -- the contractor was Sandy Block, and I never got called again for another Perex Parado date.
Yeah. But you moved on to Mercury, and I know you were really ...
Oh yeah, I moved on.

You were really -- everybody depended on you to create the sounds, whatever rhythm pattern that we were going to put behind the singer -- even the arrangers -- name some of the arrangers. We had Besford Hendrix, and ..
Oh, yeah -- we had Besford Hendrix, Burt Keys, Leroy Kirkland, Joe Mooney.
Name that young man that died that lived in New Jersey that was such a beautiful person, a West Indian black man.
An arranger?
Arranger, yeah. It'll come back to me later, but he was so instrumental in doing so many things like that.
We mentioned that Clyde Otis was the producer, and we mentioned Bedford Hendrix and Leroy Kirkland, Joe Mooney --
Joe Mooney, yeah ... oh God, I
should have brought that thing -- I got a thing at home that I can bring with a whole list of names on that.
Oh, yeah, for Clyde Otis -- like "What a Difference a Day Makes" for Dinah. He even did that great song for Nat King Cole, which he did in California -- I can't -- was it "I Can't Stop Loving You"?
No, it was a country and western song.
Country and western song, yeah, and it was a beautiful song that Nat did.
Yeah, da dee dum -- some kind of rose, I think it was.
Yeah, it was "Ramblin' Rose".
"Ramblin' Rose"! Yeah, that's it.

Oh yeah, it was a tremendous million seller. You know, it's a joy to do these things with you, because it takes two of us who have been around together to really kind of tell the whole story, so if I could just kind of enlighten your mind to some extent. Because you were really doin' it, man.
Yeah, yeah -- you can refresh my memory on some of these things.

But I was there, and you really were the guiding light in setting up these different rhythms and backgrounds, because the arrangers were writing out the string parts and would write out the harmonic parts for the band, but they left it to the rhythm section to decide what
kind of rhythm was gonna go with this, and you being the captain, or the quarterback of the rhythm section, it was you who did the decisions.

I tried to get a job as a producer, you know, behind this, but it never materialized, so I guess, like a lot of people think, playing musicians can't be producers because we don't think like producers, see.

Well, that's quite true, they might think that, and in some cases, that might be true, but there was also another element of it, too, because we had no record companies of our own, as black musicians, and we worked for other companies, and it was kind of hard, kind of difficult for us to get into that end of the business.

That's another thing I tried to do, and I don't know whether you know it or not, but I started out with Atlantic Records when they were in a loft on 54th Street and 8th Avenue. The company was owned at that time by Herb Abramson and his wife, Miriam -- and Ahmet Ertegun Nesuhi, and his brother, Lester, was in Washington -- they were just two young European boys who were living in Washington, because their father was the Ambassador or something from Turkey, and they were interested in rhythm-and-blues and jazz -- and that's where I met them, in Washington. But they hadn't even come with the company when I started recording with Atlantic -- they came in later, and then they brought Jerry Wexler in

after that -- he came in later on. But I started out with Atlantic Records, and I tried to get -- after I saw what was happening, that Atlantic was making all this money with these hits that they had, songs on the charts and everything, which was another thing that was just being started -- by Variety and the different magazines, of putting songs on charts.
I went to the guy -- I went to Mickey Baker, Sam Taylor, Ernie Hays, Lloyd Trotman, and I said to them, I said, 'Well, look, man, why can't we start a record company of our own?'
Now wait a minute -- I want you to define these guys. Mickey Baker was the hot guitarist then, right?
Guitar player, that's right.
He was the background. You were the drummer.
I was the drummer. Ernie Hays was on piano.
Sam Taylor was a hot tenor player and Lloyd Trotman was one of the base players.

Right, he was one of the base players, but he was the other one they used to do on the dates. But I tried to get them to start a record company of our own, and the answer I got from them was, 'Man, I ain't got no time for that. I'm not a businessman anyway; I'm a musician' --
so it never materialized.
Uh huh.
But I think we could have gotten something started back then.
It was unfortunate that you all couldn't get together, but a couple of guys did finally -- Clyde Otis broke through. Johnny Pate broke through in Chicago, and a couple more guys.
And Berry Gordy went to Detroit and upset everybody.
But man, this was a fabulous era, and you were doing at least 3 record dates every day.
Oh, yeah; easy.
And I'm sure you were receiving some nice checks, which you probably just got recently as a result of that.
Yeah, as a result of that.
So that's good. So could you think of any more, and if you want to continue along that line, I'd appreciate your talking more about that. Because you stayed with that until the sixties.
Around '64. Well, that's when I was having my problems at home, and I started walking in on record dates screaming at people, and well, I was just all mixed up - and the phone stopped ringing.

Plus, they were trying to find someone anyway -- to replace me, they brought in Gary Chester. Gary Chester came in and he brought in the [byonne] rhythm -- everything was [byonne,] and that's when it started changing over from actually the church rhythm that I was playing and that Joe Marshall was playing -- that's when it started becoming a technical thing, and they started going, instead of being like American rhythm-and-blues, it became Latin- black oriented.
Now Gary Chester was a drummer?
Yeah, Gary Chester was a drummer. [And his father was a drummer.]
He used to be a sub for Ray McKinelly when Ray had his big band.
Right.
Anf he would just play the solos, and Gary Chester would play the songs. Of course he was replaced later on by Purdy.
By Purdy, right. (Bernard Purdy -- ed.)

And the whole thing changed -- I certainly was replaced by the fender base, which came in, and I'm not a fender base player, and there were some great players then, though. What was that one that just died? Bob Bushnell, a very excellent fender base player and who were some of the others -- what's that guy's name who went to California?
Oh, yeah, I forgot his name now --
he is in California now. I can't remember. And then this young kid, Dud Bascomb? (Wilbur Bascomb -- ed.)
Dud Bascomb, Doug Baskin, yeah. His father's name was Doug Baskin also. What band was he in?
It was Erskine Hawkins' band. He's the guy that played that trumpet solo on "Tuxedo Junction" that everybody has to copy.
Right. And his son is one of the most excellent fender base players, and also acoustical base players, and a fine young man. Excellent young man.
(Interruption)

And while riding on the plane, it came to me that the mother of the child in California -- her brother, I met him when he first came out of the service in 1946, and he and his wife were going to Phoenix, Arizona to live. So I

got off the plane, and I asked the skycap this guy for him, and I used his name and asked for him, and this young man said to me, he said, 'Why, he is the exalted ruler of my lodge' -- he meant the Elks.
Uh huh.
And he also said, that 'His wife taught me in school,' and I said, 'Well, no kidding? Well, how can I get in touch with him?' and he said, 'Well, he's listed in the telephone book'.

So I went to the telephone book, and I called the number, and it just so happened that he was home. So I said to him -- well, I can tell you his name, his name was James McElroy. Mackleroy. So I said, 'Is this Mr. McElroy?' -- and he said, 'Yes', and I said, 'Well, I'm a friend of your sister's' and I didn't want to come out and let him know who I was, as I didn't know if he was gonna get mad or shoot me through the telephone or what.

So I acted like I was just a friend of his sister, and I said that I was in the service and I had just gotten out and was in Los Angeles trying to find his sister, but she wasn't there. So he said, 'Oh, no -- she's been living here since then and now she's living up north in California', and I said, 'Yeah? Well, how is her daughter. She had a little girl, didn't she?' and he said, 'Oh yes, she's fine -- she just finished at the University of California at Berkeley and she has a job there at the school as a student coordinator'.

"No kidding?" I said to him. I said, "Well, look, I might as well be honest with you and let you know who I am -- my name is Dave Francis, the drummer." And he said, "I thought that was you -- with that stuttering, I thought it was you!". So I said, "Well, you know, that was just one of those things that happened", and he was rather nice about it and he said to me, he said, "Well, look, I don't think you raped my sister or held a gun to her and made her to what she did; she did it because she wanted to so that was the result from it."

So I said, "Yeah, but you know, I didn't help with the kid or nothing like that; the reason for that was we had an argument at the time; a misunderstanding, and I walked away mad and she walked away mad, and that was the end of that. But now I sure would love to see her."
So anyway, he arranged it so I was able to meet her. (CUT)
But there was a funny thing that happened. I didn't know that her mother had told her that her father had died in the war. So this child was under the impression ...
Oh, her mother told her that?

Had told her that, yeah. So this child is under the impression that I was dead. Now no one told me when her mother allowed me to come there and meet her -- and I mean, I really thought this was a pretty mean thing to do.
Wait a minute now. I thought her mother's brother arranged for you to meet her.
He arranged for me to meet her through her mother; she was living with her mother.
So you called her mother.
I called her mother, and her mother told me it was all right for me to come up and meet her, see.
Oh, now I got it.

Her mother said it was all right for me to meet her. But she didn't tell me that she had told the kid that I was dead. So I go up there and I meet her, and she was very warm; she even hugged me and shook my hand, so when I got ready to leave, I told her it was nice to meet her and everything, and she said, 'well, it's nice meeting you, too' and she kissed me on the cheek and left. Well, I thought all along that the kid knew who I was, so when I get to San Francisco that night, I thought about it and I looked at her and she was such a fine young lady with a lot of class; in fact ...
How old was she then?

She was 24. And she was everything that I thought that I would want one of my daughters to be. So, the next day, I wanted to talk to her once more, so I got on the phone and made a long distance call down to where she was living with her mother, and she answered the phone, and

I said, "Hello, how you been?" and so she said, "Oh fine -- who is this?", and I said, "This is your father". And she said, "My who?" and I said, "This is your father", and she said, "Wait a minute; I think you must be crazy or something."

And I said, "Crazy? What do you mean? Where's your mother?" "She's sleeping", she said. I said, "Well, you mean to tell me your mother didn't tell you who I was?" and she said, "Yeah, she told me that you were a friend of hers." I said, "A friend of hers? Oh no, wait a minute", and then I felt awful bad, because here I was under the impression that she knew who I was, and she was under the impression that her father was dead.

And so here I come out of the clear blue sky saying to her, "This is your father". So anyway, it was a big shock to her; it really shook her up very bad, and I felt awful bad about it, and I gave her mother hell because I told her that I didn't think that was right, for her to allow me to walk in there without letting me know that this kid didn't know who I was, because I would have turned it around, and said let her find out her way who I am. it would be fine to go along with who she said I was. You know?
But anyway, we got to be rather good friends, she and I; in fact, when she got ready to get married, I helped to sponsor her wedding. Then the following year ...
Wait, did we record her name on here?
Michelle. Her name is Michelle.
And her mother's name?
Her mother's name is Mary. So now I'm with a show and playing in Toronto, Canada. I had the address of Carol in Montreal.
Who's Carol?
Carol is the mother of my baby daughter, who we called Penny, because she was very small and we called her Penny.
And that was in Montreal?
Montreal, Canada.
Uh huh.

I happened to have the phone number, I mean the address, of where she lived in Montreal, but there was a family that lived right next door to them, also, that I knew about, and I had been trying to find her, the same as I was trying to find Michelle, and so I arrived in Toronto on a Sunday, and so I didn't have anything to do, because you know up there in Canada on a Sunday, they had the blue laws and everything was closed.

So I'm laying up in bed, and it finally dawned on me, why don't you go to the phone company and look in the Montreal phone book and see if you can find that they are still listed. So I look in the listings, and I didn't see a Jones in there, so I thought about this family that lived
next door, who was the Sealy family. So I look in the phone book, and there it was and the address was right next door -- one address was 769 and the other 767, so I knew I was on the right track.
Yeah ...

So I got on the phone and called long distance, and I said, 'Hello? I'm a friend of Carol's, and I'm trying to find her; can you tell me how I can get in touch with her?' So this young lady that answered the phone said, 'Well, Carol don't live here any more. She's living in the states -- in Detroit, since she got married, and she is now living in Detroit.' I said, 'Wait?' and she said, 'yeah'. So I say, 'Well, look; let me tell you who I am'. So I told her that I was the baby's father, Penny's father, and she said, 'What? Well, she'll be sure glad to hear from you, because she always talks about you.' I say, 'she does? Well, how can I get in touch with her?'

So she gave me her address, and I wrote a letter to this address, and I told her, you know, that I had been trying to find her and I finally got this address to write her, and that I would like to see her daughter, to see what she looked like; that I wanted to see Penny. And if she got this letter to please call me; I would be in Cleveland at the hotel there, at the Sherrington Hotel.
Oh yeah.
So, as fate would have it, she got

the letter, and she called me. And it was a big shock to hear her voice again, and so she told me that she was married; that she had married a fellow -- she tried to get in touch with me before it happened, but that the baby was adopted; the fellow adopted the baby, that they had written me at Cab's office, but I had never gotten the letter, telling me that they had adopted her.
Who? Her husband adopted the baby?
Yes. Her name is Penny Gibson.
Uh huh.

So anyway, I said to her, I said, 'Well, is there any way possible that I could see her? I would just like to see what she looks like; I'd like to meet her so in case I should be walking down the street and see somebody trying to take advantage of her, at least I'll know who she is and I could sort of run to her rescue'.

So she said, 'Well, if you are able to come through Detroit, I will make arrangements so you can meet her'. She said that she lived alone, she had her own apartment and everything and you could go by there and see her. So I said okay. So I went to the airline and I made arrangements to stop -- because I was still living in Los Angeles, so I made arrangements that I could stop in Detroit for three hours before going to Los Angeles, so that was how I met Penny.
Oh, that's really interesting.
So then -- I'm not finished yet --

so then, about nine months later, I'm looking at the TV in Los Angeles, and this black woman who is the news commentator -- her last name is Williams. Now, I had another young lady that I had the third daughter by -- her name was Tara, and her brother -- I didn't know it at the time, but her brother was the lead singer with the Platters, and I was making all their records and their albums and everything, recording them all the time -- but I didn't know that this was her brother; although, I remember that when I was with her, she'd always talk about her little brother, and they used to call him Sugar Man, and his name was Tony -- Tony Williams, lead singer for the Platters.

So, anyway, I saw one of the singers, because they all lived out there in California anyway; I saw one of the singers that used to be with the Platters, at a party. And we got to talking, and I told him the story, and he said, 'Well, do you look at Channel 7?' -- and I said, 'Yeah', and he said, 'Well, that newscaster -- that woman newscaster is Tony's ex-wife. She should know how to get in touch with his sister.'

So I wrote her a letter at the station, with my phone number, and, as fate would have it, she got the letter and called me up and told me how to get in touch with Clara. So I wrote Clara a letter and told her that I had been trying to find her and Sandra -- this is my other daughter, Sandra,
and to my surprise ...
Did you know her name was Sandra?
Yeah, I knew her name was Sandra because when she was three months old, her mother brought her by for me to see her.
Oh, I see.
Yeah, so I knew her name was Sandra. So I received this letter from Clara, and she told me she was glad to hear from me, and that Sandra was the mother of six girls alone.
Wow!
And, that ...
How old was she then?

Sandra was 29 at that time -- she had six daughters of her own, and was living in the Bronx, in New York. I said, 'Well, is there any way I can get in touch with her?' and she said, 'Yes', because one thing about Clara, Clara was always a nice person -- she was very nice about it; she said, 'Well, this is something that happened between us and didn't hold it against me', so when I came to New York, I got in touch with Sandra, and I met her -- that was the first time I had seen her since she was 3 months old; she was 29 then, and I met her six daughters, and everybody was calling me 'Grandpa' for the first time. It was quite a feeling.
I mean, that was part of my love life.
You had quite a life there.

Congratulations. Say, look, you got such a magnificent resume here. Would you like to read this and we'll just talk about it, because I think everybody should know about all of the -- especially these studio recordings; the hits you played on, just tell them some of the hits you played on. Just tell them.

we did quite a few thing with him down at RCA together, didn't we?

Yeah, I think so.
Yeah, and then I did "Stupid Cupid" with Connie Francis; also, "Who's Sorry Now?" I did "Venus" with Frankie Avalon, and "From Bobby Socks to Stockings."
These were all hit records?

All these were hit records. I did Fabian's first hit record, "Like a Tiger." And I did "These Things Remind Me of You" with Della Reese; I did "Haunting Melody" with Sarah Vaughn, which is the only million selling record she ever made; I did, "What's the Matter, Baby," with [Timmie Yuro.]
Yeah, from California. I think I was on that, too.
Yeah, with Clyde Otis.
Yeah, Clyde Otis. Right.
At the Fine Sounds.
Yeah, the Fine Sounds Studio. It's not even there any more; the hotel is gone.

That's right. And the arrangement with Burt Keith. That's the first time that they used a mike on a bass drum. Was on that record. "What's The Matter, Baby?" That's when they put the mike on the bass drum, was on that record.
Huh? Is that so?

Yeah, on "What's The Matter, Baby." That's it. And I did "Lonely Boy" with Paul Anka and "You Are My Destiny" with Paul Anka, and "Patricia," which we spoke about earlier; I told you how I suggested to set up the rhythm on the overdub.
Oh, yes. But say that again, because that's worth repeating.
Well, what happened -- these were some tapes that was sitting up on the shelf.
This was the first overdub.

Right, the first overdub. There were these tapes sitting up on the shelf that Perez Prado had recorded out in California. So they brought the tapes in to New York to Herman Diez, who was the A+R man at the time at RCA.
RCA Victor.

Right. So, he got Billy Muir to write a part for himself on guitar and also for Alan Hannon to play on the bass guitar -- and this was the first time that they used a bass guitar. Not a Fender bass -- bass guitar. And I was on drums. So, we played one of the tunes, and we tried to overdub and it didn't work and we tried another tune, and the last tune we tried was "Patricia," and it was still the same thing with no results.

So, Herman said, "Well, I guess we can't do anything with this" -- and that's when I got the bright idea, because I was always suggesting something -- a lot of the guys in the studio used to tell me to keep my mouth shut, but I just couldn't sit there and know that something could happen you know, if I made a suggestion and tried it, it just may work.

So, I suggested that Billy Muir play this rhythm on the tambourine that I showed him to play, and then let Alan Hannon play what he was playing on the bass guitar, and I would play a straight 8 with a backbeat on the drums with the brushes.
Would you demonstrate just tap that out, and Panama? give me an idea. That sounds great.
(Demonstrates drum, bass guitar, and tambourine parts)
Yeah, and so we played about eight bars, and Herman said, "Let's make it". And that's how "Patricia" was born.
That was a big hit for Perado.
Oh, it sold almost two million records, and they're still playing it. I got $41 to the quarter for that, by the way.
Who played trumpet on that, because he had a lot of high trumpet players on that.
That was in California. With some band out in California where they recorded.
Oh, I see, and you all just overdubbed it in New York then.
Yeah, overdubbed it in New York. Right. That's what happened.
I see. So go on.
So then I did 'Don't Let Go,' with Roy Hamilton. This is another one -- 'Love is Strange.'
Who was the arranger on the Roy Hamilton number? Do you remember?
Jesse Stone.
Uh huh.
Jesse Stone was the arranger on that, yeah. Then we did 'Love is Strange' with Mickey and Sylvia.
Yeah. What was Mickey's name? Mickey ...
Mickey Baker.
Mickey Baker. Then he went to Europe and stayed there ...
He's still there; he's in France, Paris.

And there was something that was lacking in the making of the record, in the record, and they didn't know what it was, so I suggested to let me play a cow bell. We played about four bars and we made the record, and it sold in the millions. Another hit record.

Then I did "Jim Dandy" with Laverne Baker, I did "My Prayer" with the Platters, "Twilight Time," "Stardust," "Only You," "The Great Pretender," "Smoke Gets In Your Eyes" -- all of these were made with the Platters.
With the Platters, wow ...
Then I did "Baby Work Out," "Reek-a-Teek," "Reet Petite," "Night," and "Danny Boy," with Jackie Wilson. As a matter of fact, I made all of his records.
Yeah, I think I was on quite a few of those myself.
You were there with me, that's right.
Did you ever do anything with the Ravens? Remember that quartet?
The Ravens? No, I never recorded with them.
No?

No, never recorded with them. That one I missed. Then I did "Earth Angels" with a group out in California called the Penguins, that was a big hit for them. Then I did "Endlessly" with Brook Benton, "Just a Matter
of Time // -- you were on these things.
Yeah, we joined each other then.

That's right. And Fools Rush In, everybody was talking about that rhythm that was played on Fools Rush In, and the rhythm that I used on that, was a hillbilly -- like the hillbilly would play on the guitar, which they call country music today, but in those days, it was called hillbilly music, and I played the rhythm, that the rhythm guitar player would be playing on the hillbilly music, I played that rhythm with my brushes on Fools Rush In, which went something like this ... (tapping on desk)
Oh, I see.
That was the rhythm. And everybody was talking about that rhythm.
I remember Clyde Otis, I had a lot of respect for him, because you and I both worked with Clyde Otis when he was making demo records, and Brook Benton was a demo singer.
A demo singer, right.
So he carried you on with him when he went in to production and he carried me in there, but I remember, and he had Besford Hendricks who was his friend.
Yeah, he really was pretty nice about that; he looked out for his own people, you know?
Yeah, and you were very helpful to him, because he would make the arrangements, but he would let
you set the rhythm pattern, and we worked; you and Ernie Hays...

Yeah, but you know, he got angry with me because I -- and I'm not a businessman, I guess, and I don't think that way, but he thought I should have made more money than I did, instead of passing it on to somebody else, you know?
But at the time, I just didn't see it, I just didn't think about it, to be honest with you; I didn't bother with it.
Well, who are you speaking of in that term?

Well, as a contractor. I gave the contracting to somebody else; he wanted me to be the contractor, and I said, I don't want it, and at the time, I gave it to Frank Carroll because I was doing all of Frank Carroll's work. So instead of me making the money, Frank Carroll was making the money and I was getting $5 and a quarter, I think it was at that time.
Yeah, but you really set those rhythm patterns, because Ernie Hays and Everett Barksdale.
Yeah, and Carl Lynch.
You know, I saw Carl the other day, and man, he looked marvelous -- it was just so good to see him.
Oh yeah?
Yeah, it was a long time since I'd seen him. Man, what a list.

And then I did "What a Difference a Day Makes" with Dinah Washington. Now that was another one that everyone was talking about the rhythm, and the rhythm on that was the press rolls with the brushes -- that was what that was. Instead of playing like that with the sticks, I played with the brushes. (Demonstrates) And that sold; that was a big hit. And then I did "Drowning in My Own Tears" with Ray Charles. Now that was quite an experience for me, because Ray was the one who pulled my coat how to taught me to play the brushes like in the church, with a Gospel feeling.
And all I played, I'm telling you ...
How'd he do that?

It is so simple; it is so simple that you wouldn't believe it. All I played was just straight quarter notes. He sang said ... "It brings me tears" -- chat's all I played with those brushes. Because if you remember, in the church, that was the way the mothers used to keep the babies quiet on their knees when they were singing; all they did was lift their foot and then drop it -- just a straight 4-4, that's all they were doing, and the baby, they'd be patting the baby and they'd go right back to sleep. And that's what I was playing on the drums with Drowning In My Own Tears." (Demonstrates)
And Ray suggested that, huh?
Yeah, he suggested it, and showed me how to do it, too; he came over to the drums and showed me how it was done, and I did it, and I was really thrilled about that.

Then I did "I Put a Spell On You" for Screaming Jay Hawkins. Now that was the first time they used the 12/8 rhythm. They had been using like 4/4 and the 6/8 9/8 rhythm for the Gospel tunes, but they had never used a 12/8 rhythm before on a rock and roll record, rhythm and blues record, they called them at that time. And that was done like, da, da, da ...\ (demonstrates) "I Put a Spell On You -- Because You're Mine," remember that?
Oh, yeah ...
But that was the first time -- "I Put A Spell on You with Screaming Jay Hawkins. Then I did, "Where Are You" with Dinah Washington.
"Where Are You? Yeah, I did that, too.
That's right, you were there on bass. Then I did "Wild One" with Bobby Rydell, and I did the "Tea For Two Cha Cha" with Warren Covington, which was a big hit for him.

I did "I Worry About You" with Arthur Prysock, I did "All in the Game" with Tommy Edwards, "Everybody's Somebody's Fool;" I did that with Connie Francis, I did "Lavender Blue" with Sammy Turner, I did "The Lion Sleeps Tonight" with the Tokens, I did "Peggy Sue" with Buddy Holly, who they made a movie of his life, but I wasn't called in to that.

Corina " with Joe Turner, the great blues singer; I did "Tossing and Turning" with Bobbie Lewis; I did "Talk to Me" and "Fever" with Little Billy John; I did "Cloudburst" with Sam "the Man" Taylor which was a big hit; I did I Only Have Eyes for You with the Flamingoes; I did the "Hawaiian Wedding Song" with Andy Williams, I did Green Green with the Christy Minstrels.
This is just a list of some of the things that I did.
That's just amazing. There wasn't many that you missed that was recording at that time; you really went through them all. I don't know of anybody who could top that list.
Hey, let's talk about some of the tenor players -- now we're both in the rhythm section what with my whiskey voice and your fingers, which I hope people will appreciate.
(CUT)
Yeah, we're talking about rhythm. Now who were some of these guys; you mentioned some of the guys that really was making all these funny sounds that we needed to put on top behind these singers.

Yeah, but the funny thing about that -- these guys weren't making funny sounds; guys like Sam Taylor, who were playing what they called bootin' tenor, you know bootin' tenor; it wasn't all these wild, funny sounds.
No, I didn't mean to imply ...
No, I'm just saying -- like there was
Sam Taylor, Red Prysock, Al Sears, [Count Hasty], these were the tenor players that were used ...
What about King Curtis?
King Curtis came later. But he copied Sam; he even admits that he copied Sam Taylor. Then he came up with a different thing called the chicken sound.
Yeah, the chicken sound. But that was more or less original with him, wasn't it?

Yeah, that was original. That was him, and he did that on "Charlie Brown." He played that sound. But with Sam Taylor and Red Prysock and these guys, they were playing blues changes, I mean and the basic, not the modern blues changes, but the basic blues changes -- that's what these guys were playing. And then King Curtis came later on with "Charlie Brown," with this chicken sound and it seemed like all the tenor players that couldn't play this type of horn like Sam Taylor and Red Prysock and then, latched on to this chicken sound, and so that's how it became popular.
Now this Red Prysock -- what was his name?
Yeah, Red Prysock -- Prysock, the singer's, brother.
Yeah, what was his name, Al? One was Red Prysock.
Yeah, one was named Red and the other one was named Arthur.
Arthur Prysock! Yeah.
Arthur Prysock, and his brother was Red.
Red, yeah. And then there was also another trumpet player, remember this cat, Sil Seal Austin?
Sil Seal Austin. Yeah, that's right, Sil Seal Austin was another one. Another one who came later.
Yeah, so we had a variety of them to give different species aspects to the sound.
Right, but there's one thing; they all played a swinging type of horn.
Yeah, Sam Taylor was mighty mellow.
Yeah, well, he was the boss. He was the boss.
Yeah, he really captured a great beat. I can see Sam now walking in to the studio and opening up his sax0aphone case with his gin in there.
Gin, that's right. And he would turn around and say, 'going up!'

Can you elaborate on that a little more, Panama? Because it's been so interesting so far. Let me see, you mentioned all of these different hit songs. You mentioned Fabian and Della Reese and Sarah Vaughn, you mentioned all of them, didn't you?
Yes, I did. Yeah. Although some of them I forgot.
Well, here in 1974, who was that now?

Well, in 1974 I toured England, with Warren Covington playing the music with Tommy Dorsey. And we also had Sy Oliver with him, because you know, Sy Oliver was the arranger for that. 'Yes Indeed,' and all those.
'Yes, Indeed' and 'Cheating On Me,' and 'You're a Cute Little Tootie,' and all of those things. And during the same year, I got a chance to go with Ray Conniff to England.
Now, there's one thing I have to say; that Ray Coniff has been faithful, even up to this date. I was just in South America with him. But I did his first recording date.
Let the people who know who Ray Conniff was; of course, I know he was a trombone player.

Well, Ray Conniff was a trombone player and also he was a top staff arranger at Columbia at the time; he was staff arranger and he was writing for Johnny Mathis -- in fact, that's his arranger on 'Chances Are,' which people are still playing and was a big hit for Johnny Mathis.
Yeah, and he was also the arranger for with Mitch Miller, wasn't he?

He was also the arranger for Mitch Miller, yes. In fact, this was how he got the chance to do this album; he kept worrying Mitch until one day Mitch told him it was all right to go ahead and do this album.
What was the album like?

Well, he had an idea of using voices like horns, you see, using voices like horns. Like, he liked the high voices of women, and they were the trumpets, and the low voices was the men. And so he came in with this drum part, which if I had played it the way it was written, it would never have happened. So I made a rhythm of my own with the brushes, and I mean, the only thing it was, it was the same rhythm I would play with sticks on the cymbal, but instead I was playing it on a snare drum, and it worked.

And so, from then on, I did all of his sessions using this rhythm. And even when he got ready to move out to California, he wanted me to gowith him, but I didn't go, but then again, every drummer out there hated me because he wanted them to play the same as I did on the record, and he lost a lot of friends who were drummers out in California because of that. But whnever he got ready to make a tour of any kind, he always got in touch with me, and I would go on tours with him, so I was with him in 1974 in England, which we had a great success there.
And, I also went the following year -- 1975, I went to Japan with him.
Oh? You did?
Yeah, I was in Japan with him. And then in 1976, I went to South America with him.
You went left in 1976?
Yeah.
I thought it was '78. Last year.
No, this is '78 now, right? No, then it was 1977 I went to South America.
Yeah, and you also went to Japan with Sam Taylor a couple of times, didn't you?

Oh, I went with Sam Taylor five times to Japan. In fact, I played 72 cities in Japan -- one time we were there for 6 weeks, and we played from the top, north, from Wakinai all the way down to Nakasaki -- 72 cities. I never worked that hard in my life! Other than working with Lionel Hampton.

... they had a Drum and Bugle Corps, and every other Sunday, they would have a parade, and so at the age of 8, I joined this Drum and Bugle Corps. We had a drum teacher there, Mr. McCullen, David McCullen, who was an ex army man from World War I that used to teach us all the different drum beats pieces. And I would learn mine by ear, because I didn't know anything about reading any music, and I don't think he knew too much himself about reading music. But anyway, whatever the rhythms he would play on the marches or the rhythms he'd play on the drum, we all would learn it. By the time I was 9 years old, I had worked myself up to be the number one drummer over all of the older boys that was there. And they also had a marching band that was a part of the UNIA, which I joined around about 9 1/2 years old. But there also was another -- in fact, Miami had like, there was a St. Agnes Marching Band, there was a St. Mary's Marching Band, there was a Masonic Marching Band, and the UNIA had a band. And every Sunday there was a parade -- somebody had a parade; either one of the lodges or one of the churches had a funeral or something like that, because back in those days, in Miami, if you didn't have a band at your funeral, you
were a nobody. I mean you had to have a band at your funeral; that meant that you were somebody.

So anyway, every Sunday there was something going on. So I joined the UNIA band, and from there, that's how I got the chance to meet Brother Roberts, because see, he was the musical director of St. Agnes's band which was the number one band around Miami. They used to play for the churches, and almost all of the lodges.
So I joined St. Agnes' band, too, so I was playing with the UNIA band and I also was playing with St. Agnes' band.

And then from there, there was a man that lived a couple of doors down from us that belonged to the Church of God, Mr. Chipman, who played a cello, and he used to play the bass parts in church with the piano, and him on cello, and the people in church would play the tambourine and the bass drum, so that's how I came in -- I used to play the bass drum on Sundays, although I belonged to the Roman Catholic faith, that was my gig on Sunday -- I used to go to the church and play, and I used to get 50¢ for playing there. It'd be like, all day Sunday.

So anyway, we also used to play for the -- when they got baptized, we used to have to march from, like, 5th and Court Corbin and 17th Street to where the church was, to almost Miami Beach where the water was, and that's where they had the Baptisms there, and we used to march back to the church from there.
So I played, between the UNIA Marching Band and St. Agnes Marching Band, I played with these two until I reached the age of around 12½.

And I'll never forget, I played my first gig -- it was on the fourth of July, at the UNIA Hall in 1931, and I wasn't 13 yet -- I wasn't 13 until that December. And I did so well, until I was asked by a fellow around Miami, a saxophone player named Sonny Boy, and Sonny Boy asked my mother if I could join his group, which was working at the barbecue stand on 3rd Avenue and 14th Street -- it was sort of a juke joint, and we used to play there five nights a week, and each night, there was either a good shooting scrap or a cutting scrape or something. This was where all the bad type of people used to come. And that's where we played at.
This was where I formed that fondness for upright pianos, because many a night when they got to shooting, that was where the whole band could be found -- behind the piano.
What do you mean by a juke joint? What is a juke joint?

Well, that was because whenever we played, like, a slow blues, the men and the women would be out on the floor like they were having sex, only they were standing up then and had their clothes on. But that was the only difference. And that's why it was called a juke joint.
Oh, I see.
And my mother used to take me there

and wait for me until the end of the night and bring me home.

And I'll never forget the first song I ever played -- it was "Blue Prelude"; we played that, and we used to play "Dinah" and "Sweet Sue" and "One Sweet Letter from You" and all those types of tunes then.

So I stayed there, and there was a band -- I was still in school at the time, and there was a band with a bunch of school kids that was under the direction of Mr. Leander Kirksey, Kurtzin who was responsible for Nat Adderley and Cannonball Adderley, and he had just come out of college in Florida A&M, and he came down to Miami to teach at Booker Washington High School.

And the trumpet section, we had a fellow who I still

Well, we used to play every Saturday night at a dance hall up at Ft. Well, there was a guy that used to come there every other Saturday -- he would come, and as soon as he would get drunk, the first thing he'd do was come up to the bandstand and knock a hole in my base drum. And I used to get so mad, but I had to smile because back in those days, you had better smile, so I smiled, but I didn't like it too well.

But then he would give me $5. Well, at that time, drums heads, you had to buy them loose -- they wasn't already tucked on to the drum, and so I was able to go to the music store down there on Flagley Street -- the music store was owned by Mr. Armandon and his wife, and he would sell me a base drum head for $3. So I used to make $2 on the deal every other week.
So, anyway, I would go over and take this drum head home and soak it in one of those number three tubs until it got soft, and I would take a spoon and ...
What's a number three tub, Panama?
That's a wash tub. That's what you used to bathe in all the time; they didn't have no bathtubs.
Well, how come they had numbers on them?

Sure. It was number one and number three was the big one. So I used to take the number three tub and soak my drum head in it, and then I would get a spoon and get out on the back porch and I would tuck it and then put it onto the bass drum.

An eating spoon, a spoon that you eat with, you used the handle of the spoon to tuck the drum head on to the rim. That's how you used to do it.
Oh, I see. Yeah.
Yeah, and tuck it on to the rim.
Like putting a tie on or something.

That's right, and this was the same principle. it'd be smooth, and then you put it on to the drum, and you'd put it on just enough so that the rim would hold it, because when it dried, it would tighten up and then you would put some more water on it so it would loosen up a bit and then you would turn the bolts around to tighten it up a little more.
And this was how you used to have to put the bass drum head on.

Oh, it would take about a day.
I see.

Come by the day or night after you died?
No, they come by the night before the funeral, because they used to bring you home. They would bring the body home and have it in the living room, in a

corner of the house there, and all your friends would come in and -- say, they bring in the body at about five o'clock that evening, and they would start coming in around about five minutes after five, they would stop in and look at you, because they would have the casket open.

And they would sing hymns, they would talk about you and say, "Yeah, look at him laying up there -- remember the time he did such and such ..." and everybody would laugh about it, and they would tell different stories about him and they would drink and they would eat and go to sleep.
