Uh huh.

Now, like when St. Agnes's band used to play all these funerals -- we would meet at the hall, at the rehearsal hall where the band used to rehearse at, which was the parish hall of St. Agnes Church. We would meet there, and say, the funeral was going to start at two o'clock -- well, we would meet at 12:30, the band would meet there, and naturally you belonged to a couple of lodges -- at least one lodge. So the band would assemble at the parish hall and march down to the lodge hall, and go to the lodge hall -- all the lodge members would be there, and would line up, and then we would march back to the home to pick up the body.

Now we were liable to play any of Sousa's marches, going to the lodge hall and going to the home, but now, when we leave the home with the body, we take the snares off the drum, which was a field drum, and took the snares off and took a handkerchief and put the handkerchief around the snares so there would be no vibration at all - just a dead sound.
And we would play a tune like "Free as a Bird," you know, dum da da da, da -- we would play that, or we would play "Abide With Me" -- a tune like that, and march slowly to the church.

Now, while the service is going on, see, all of the musicians, and there was a lot back there -- this was during the time of Prohibition, it was still Prohibition, see, and all of the guys in the band would go to one of the moonshine houses where they sold moonshine, and everybody would be sitting up there, because they would leave one guy that didn't drink; they would leave him so he could keep up with the service and let them know what time to get back.
Uh huh.
And so he would sit there, and a lot of them would drink so much that by the time the service was over, they could hardly walk!
But anyway, this is what would happen. They would come back, and they would take the body out of the church, and we would march to a slow dirge slowly until we got almost to the White town,
Right where the boundary line was.
What was White town?

Well, the White town at that time was like, 21st Terrace and 6th Avenue. So that's where we were stopped. And they would open up an aisle, like the band would split and half of one side and one on the other side, and the lodge members; all of those that wasn't going to the graveyard, they would all do the same thing.

And the cars would slowly drive through while we would still play this dirge; piece, they would slowly go through until the last car got through there, and that's when the drummer would roll off and would either play "The Saints" or "Onward Christian Soldiers." We never played Ditty Ramble; I don't ever remember playing that.
Well, why did you come through this White town?
Well, that's where the black section of town finished.
Oh, I see.

And that's where the white section started, so we couldn't go marching through there playing the dirge, those pieces, so we stopped right here and they let the cars go. The graveyard was like about 10 miles out of town, and we had to go through White town to get there.
I see. I just wanted to mention, you
called me Pump, which is my nickname from the Cab Calloway era.
Well, I always forget about the Milton
No, that's okay. I just wanted it on the record, so they knew who that was.

Panama, you talked about drumming and when you started drumming -- were there any drummers that you heard that inspired you to want to be a drummer? I know in my case, I used to hear Duke's band come through and admired Braud Hat Brow and I thought he was a marvelous base player and I wanted to be like him. But was there anybody, any drummers that you looked up to?

Well, there was a guy in Miami, his last name was Abrista, but one night a couple of guys got in a fight, and he was from the Bahamas and he was telling the guys to let him go, but instead of saying let him go, he said, "lette go", and he got this nickname, "Lettego", and everybody used to call him Lettego and so he and my cousin Harold who was a trumpet player, and he used to play all the house parties around Miami.

And my father was a bootlegger, and like every one once a month, he would have a party at the house so he could sell his liquor, and my cousin Harold and Lettego and a banjo player named Birdie and a base player named Fletcher, they all used to play all the house parties around there.
In fact, that's when I first saw a Coca Cola bottle being used as a mute. I think I was about 6 or 7 years old at the time, but I remember it well.

And I saw him playing the drums, and he was singing, which I can't do -- but he was singing, and he also would take the megaphone and put it on the snare drum and would blow through it and he got a crazy jazz sound out of this drum with the megaphone. And that's when I decided that was for me.

Although, like my father, my father had -- he did not want me to be a musician; he was deadly against me being a musician, because my cousin Harold and Lettego and them, all they would do was sit up there and drink all night and sleep all day, and spend all the money they made -- and Daddy just thought that was not the kind of life for me, although I wish he had lived to see what happened and the end result, as far as my being a musician, because I think he would have been pretty proud to have seen what happened to me. But he passed away before all this materialized.
When you got to New York, were there any particular drummers, in other bands, that you looked up to? Who were some of them?
impressed you?
Oh, Chick
Chick Webb was my idol. I never seen the man, but I used to hear the broadcasts from the Savoy when I was in Miami. And I also saw the great Kaiser Marshall,

when he came to Miami with his band -- he brought a band to Miami, and his band was -- Jimmy Powell, the alto saxophone player; at this time, I think Jimmy was about 17 or 18 years old, and that's when I first met him -- down in Miami, with Kaiser Marshall's band.
And Kaiser Marshall really impressed me because he was a sharp dresser, and this guy really knew how to dress, and he was a real ladies' man.
He really got them, I knew him very well.

Yeah, real dapper. And that was another inspiration for me, you know, when I came to New York. And to think that although I idolized Chick Webb's playing, I never did see him in person. When I came to New York, he had taken sick and he was in the hospital, and I never had the pleasure of seeing him in person. But I heard so many great stories about him from fellows that worked with him like Tab Jordan and Elmer Williams, and they used to tell me different things that he used to do on the drums, and I would try to do the same thing when I would play.
Uh huh. Did you ever run into Zutty Singleton or Big Sid or any of those guys?
I had the pleasure of working with Zutty Singleton at the Central Plaza on Second Avenue and 6th Street for 10 years; I was like the house drummer up
there, and Zutty Singleton was the other house drummer, because they used to have two bands up there and each of them played a half hour set, and I was with Conrad Janis, who had the group up there.
Yeah, he played with them -- a trombone player.
Yeah.
Yeah, he played for him quite a bit. He was an actor or something, wasn't he?

Yeah, he was an actor, but he also was a trombone player, and so he had a group, and I played with them up there for 10 years. It was Conrad, Dick Welston, the piano player, there was Eugene Sedrick, formerly with Fats Waller, was a clarinet player, and Herman Archer, also from the Fats Waller group was the another trumpet player -- and the first time I met Big Sid Catlett was in Miami in 1935; he came there with Don Redman, and in that band was Denny Morton, Quentin Jackson was the other trombone player, and Gene Simon. There were three trombones -- Gene Simon, Denny Morton and Quintin Jackson, who we called "Brutta".
Brutta, right.

And that was the first time I had ever seen a trombone with a great big bell on it. I don't know where Denny Morton got this trombone from, but it had an extra large bell on it, you know? And it really was impressive to me.
And the piano player was a guy named Kirk-Kilpatrick, who was also a great arranger at that time around Miami.
Who was the drummer in that band?
The drummer was Big Sid.
Aha!
Yeah, that's my first time seeing him. And he spent his whole intermission talking to me, and I was very much impressed with him.
What would he say?
Well, [he'd ask me] different things about the drums, and he was trying to play -- and things I would see him do, I would ask about them, and he tried to explain them to me.

And, later on, when I came to New York, whenever he was in town, we used to hang out together every now and then, and I will never forget the time that I was out in California, and he had his own group at a club there, I think the club was called The Last Word, that was where I first saw Allen Eager -- Allen Eager was playing out there at the time.

And Sid and I used to hang out there, because at that time, he was doing very well for himself; I mean, as a leader. Then I got the pleasure of being with him again in at Wildwood, New Jersey when he was with Louis Armstrong. Louis Armstrong had Jack Teagarden T. Garden and Aurell Shore, and Earl Hines Arvell Shaw,
was the piano player.
Yeah, I think I was working there with you with Cab Calloway.
We were with Cab Calloway; we also played there, too, in Wildwood.
Yeah.

Well, Big Sid and I went fishing one day while we were there, and we both got sea sick as soon as we got out into the ocean there, and we were sick for quite awhile, but we were fortunate enough that we just pulled ourselves together and we went out there and fished, and I think that between the two of us, we caught enough fish that we had a fishfry that night after work, and everybody just had a good time on that fish... And Louis was there ...
Yeah, I remember that, man. I remember that quite well.
(Interruption)
I think Count Basie's band came to New York in 1937. Did you ever run into that band with Joe Jones in that band, when Joe Jones was playing drums there?

I ran into that band in 1939 -- in 1938, I saw the band at the Rockland Palace, that was the first time I'd seen Joe Turner, a tall, skinny guy shouting the blues, but I never was able to get -- because in fact, when I came to New York, I didn't know hardly anybody, other than a

few musicians that had played around Miami. So I was sort of shy to go up to the bandstand and introduce myself; and furthermore, there were so many people around the guys in the band, I wouldn't have gotten the chance to speak to them anyway.

But I did get a chance to meet Joe in 1939 at the Famous Door when I was playing with Roy --I had just joined Roy, and Coleman Hawkins had just come in town from Europe, and we all went over to the Famous Door to see him, and that was when I met Joe Jones.
Oh, you never saw him play with the band, then?
I saw him play with the band at the Famous Door.
Oh, the Famous Door.
Yeah, in 1939. He was still with the band then.
Hey, that's beautiful.
And I was very much impressed with him because he was such a showman. Plus, I mean, he really made that band play. He was the sparkplug.
He really set it up, huh.
Yeah.
And I think he's still known as the world's greatest rhythm section.
That's right.
Walter Page,
Count Basie, Freddie Green, and Joe Jones. The most famous one, anyway.
That's right.
Hey, in recent years, you've been doing quite a bit of traveling in Europe. How did you like Europe and who did you play with over there, Panama?

Well, my first trip over there was with Milt Buckner, and Arnett Cobb, Tiny Grimes, and a bass player from France named Roland Lavesoir, and I was very much impressed with the people in Europe by the way they accepted jazz.

And I made quite a few friends over there. Especially, like, people in France, and I have been going back there since 1973, and in fact, I'm getting ready to go there now with my own band; I'm taking my band over there in January of 1979.
Great. Have you ever been over there before?

No, I always was with someone else. Well, yes, I did. At the Jazz Festival, I played the music of Lucky Millinder there, which was in 1976, and went over very big. In fact, it was the highlight of the festival in 1976 and we played with the New York Jazz Repertoire Company.
Beautiful.
And I had done this concert before at Carnegie Hall.
Yes, I remember that.

With George Wein Williams and at the New Repertory York Jazz Repertoire Company, and it was a great sucess, and so it was repeated again in Nice. But that was the only time I had ever had a band of my own over there.
Uh huh. What countries did you seem to like best over there and what countries did you seem to like the jazz music best?

Well, I was very much impressed with the way they accepted the type of jazz that I was playing in places like France or Switzerland and Holland and Belgium. We were very successful in these places -- and also, Spain.
And how was the audience response?
Oh, the audience response was -- I often say to my friends that in Europe I'm a king and in my own country, I'm Panama Who?
How are the conditions there for traveling and living for musicians?

Well, I mean, it wasn't too good for passenger me because I'd been used to riding in 44 Greyhound busses, and they had -- what they had was one of these Fiat trucks that they put some seats in, which they used to carry the instruments in one half of it and then in the other half, they used as a bus, and it was very uncomfortable traveling like that.
Uh huh.
But as far as the hotels; I mean, the
accommodations in the hotels, there was only one time that I stayed at a hotel that I wasn't happy with. All the rest of them were very nice.
Did you play with any European bands over there?
No, I never played with any European bands -- always American musicians, all except Roland who was the bass player.
Well, we're just about getting down to the wire with this; this has been such a beautiful experience talking with you, Panama. But I'd like to ask you a couple of things.
You mentioned in January, you're going back to Europe with your own band. What is your future? What are you looking for your plans for the future in the music business? What are you looking towards?

Well, I tell you -- I consider myself, I usually look upon myself as a prostitute -- wherever the money is, that's where I'm going. If I can make money as a leader, I mean if someone wants me to -- I'm not going to put myself in the position where I would be asking someone, but if someone thought enough of me and had enough faith in me that they thought I could lead a band and thought I could do so, I'd be happy to do it.
And, if they want me to be a side man, I'd be happy
to do that.
Is there any particular type of music you'd really choose for the future to play in any particular way?

Well, I still have maintained that jazz was primarily music to dance to, and I still hold on to that theory. I feel that people should be able to not only sit and listen to jazz, but they should be able to dance to it, also, if they so choose to do so. Because this is the way it used to be and this is the way this music, to me, was founded, ton. I feel the music was founded because the people had to have something to dance to, and that's how this music came about.

Uh huh. Is there anything you would like to say in conclusion; something you would like to advise young musicians or young drummers -- what would you tell them, since this is part of your story. To wind up this thing, what advice would you give a young musician, and especially, a young drummer?

Well, I would like to tell young drummers that, since they have the opportunities that I didn't have, to try and learn as much as they can about their instrument; try and learn the drum well and if they can, try to learn how to play a little vibes, a little temp; but of all

things, go and learn how to read, how to make time -- if the man says, or whoever you work for, says to be there at eight o'clock, try to be there at a quarter of eight with your drums set up, so when eight o'clock comes, you'll be ready to hit.
Beautiful. I know a friend of yours that we didn't mention, whose should come up on here. Cozy Cole, his name came up a little while ago.
Oh, he was a sweetheart.
Yeah, he's a sweet man.

Yes, he is. But Cozy, you know, I took lessons from Cozy, when I was learning how to read, I went to Cozy, when he had a was out of school, because he was on 54th Street and 8th Avenue, and I took lessons from him for about 4 months.

Now Cozy was responsible for me getting interested in learning about rudiments, because I didn't know anything about rudiments -- I didn't know a five stroke from a seven stroke rudiment, and a rose was a rose to me, you know?

Yeah. I'm glad his name came up when we were talking about young drummers, because you said you went to him and he's always been around to kind of lend a hand to young people in the drumming business.
Oh, yes. Well, he helped me a lot as far as the technical part of drumming goes -- he was a great help to me.
Yeah. I remember one time he and the
late Gene Krupa had a little drumming school there.
That's the school I went to!
Yeah, over on 54th and 8th.
Eighth Avenue, that's the school I went to -- the Krupa, Cozy Cole Drum School.
There couldn't be two nicer guys together.
True; two sweethearts together, both of them.
Yeah.

Hey man, this is beautiful. I wanted to know, do you have some kind of final statement or anything you'd like to say just to wrap this up, because it's been a really beautiful interview, and I sure thank you for it. I'm sure sometime in the future, people will be listening to this and very much appreciating what you have said, and will be very interested to know what times were like in our day, and what we went through and how we got where we are. So just to wind up, anything you'd like to say.

Well, all I can say is that this really was a pleasure for me to backtrack and go over all the things that happened during my life as a musician, and being able to talk about some of the wonderful people that I met, and how grateful I am to a lot of them -- you, for one. I remember one time we were in Cab's band together,

and you were a little older than I was -- or am --and we had some words, and I said to you, that when I get your age, I wouldn't even be playing drums, I would be retired. And here, when I got to be the age that you were at that time, I think I came to you and I told you, I reminded you of it, and I was able to say 'Well, man, I'm still playing,' and I was just really beginning to learn how to play the drums.
I think at the time you were something like 38, and when I got to be 38, that's when I realized that I didn't know what I was doing -- I was just learning.

And all of these things; I sit back and I think about them, and all I can say it that it has been a great education for me. I learned a lot, and I hope that my life in some way will help some young fellow to come up and do as well as I did or better.

Thank you, Panama. I'm sure they will, because just this interview, with just them listening to what you've accomplished and knowing that your life is still going on and is still going to greater heights, I'm sure it's going to be very advantageous.
Thank you very much.
Panama, say your Social Security number.
And your address?
My address in New York is 626 Riverside Drive, in care of Steele, Apt. 3-4, New York City, New York, zip
And the telephone number there is 283-3908. My home in Orlando -- the number there is 433 Ventura Avenue, and that's Orlando, Florida, zip 32845. The telephone number is 423-5501.
Check.
(CUT)
(END OF PROCEEDINGS AS RECORDED)

segments.title: Smithsonian copyright notice and title page
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright warning and the Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Project title page for Reel 1, interview by Milt Hinton.

segments.title: How David Francis became 'Panama'
segments.summary: Hinton opens the interview in Nice, France; Francis explains that Roy Eldridge called him Panama at his first rehearsal because of his Panama hat.

segments.title: Birth in Miami and his Haitian and Bahamian parents
segments.summary: Born December 21, 1918 in Miami; his father Louis Francoise/Francis fled Haiti, his mother Hattie Morrison came from Nassau, and they met in Miami around 1916.

segments.title: Half-sister, siblings and first schools in Miami
segments.summary: Names his half sister Iona Roker, sister Naomi who died young, brother Louis, and the early private schools he attended.

segments.title: Father's record collection and the first record he played
segments.summary: His father collected records; he remembers the Victrola accident and his first record, Running Wild by the Ferde Grofe orchestra.

segments.title: Cousin Harold Newchurch and house-party musicians
segments.summary: His trumpet-playing cousin Harold played Miami house parties for drinks, which left his father convinced musicians were worthless.

segments.title: Honey Boys, the Della Robia and the family's Exuma and Nassau roots
segments.summary: Local bands and the Della Robia Ballroom, banjo-playing cousin Preston Marshall, and a tangled account of his mother's family and his father's South Carolina ancestry.

segments.chapter: Childhood, drums and early church bands
segments.title: Always wanting a drum; a lonely childhood and stammering
segments.summary: He wanted drums from age four or five, felt unloved by a strict mother, began stuttering after a frozen church-play speech, and found companionship in the drum.

segments.chapter: Childhood, drums and early church bands
segments.title: Drum and Bugle Corps and the Marcus Garvey UNIA band
segments.summary: At eight he joined the UNIA Drum and Bugle Corps, learning by ear; he and Hinton discuss Garvey's organising.

segments.chapter: Childhood, drums and early church bands
segments.title: Playing drums at the Church of God for 50 cents on Sundays
segments.summary: At about ten he played snare in a small church group with cello, piano and tambourines.

segments.chapter: Childhood, drums and early church bands
segments.title: His parents' unhappy marriage and separation
segments.summary: His jealous mother and outgoing father argued constantly; they separated when he was eleven.

segments.chapter: Childhood, drums and early church bands
segments.title: Joining the St. Agnes Cornet Band under Bella Roberts
segments.summary: Bella Roberts, leader of the St. Agnes band, asked his mother if the eleven-year-old could play drums with the marching band.

segments.chapter: Childhood, drums and early church bands
segments.title: His Catholic upbringing and the Garvey movement's American Catholic Church
segments.summary: He belonged to St. Peter's American Catholic Church, which his Haitian father joined through the Garvey movement.

segments.title: Father's work and how his French accent opened doors
segments.summary: His father went from construction work to spiritualist and, speaking French-accented English, could shop where other black people could not.

segments.title: A comfortable home and his father's blues records
segments.summary: He never went hungry; his father collected Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith and other records.

segments.title: Segregated Miami and Second Avenue, the black main street
segments.summary: Lynchings in Miami, and the Second Avenue shopping strip with its theatres, restaurants and Bill Rivers's Rockland Palace.

segments.chapter: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
segments.title: First house-party gig with Bella Roberts
segments.summary: His first gig at about eleven was a house party with Bella Roberts on trumpet, Gladys Roberts on piano and Milton Fletcher on bass.

segments.chapter: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
segments.title: Becoming the family meal ticket and the Barbecue Stand
segments.summary: After his parents separated, his mother put him to work; at twelve he played four nights a week in a rough barbecue joint, ducking behind the piano during shootings.

segments.chapter: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
segments.title: Joining George Kelly's Cavaliers and who was in the band
segments.summary: At about fourteen he joined teenage band George Kelly and his Cavaliers, rival to Hartley Toots's Orange Pickers; he lists the members.

segments.chapter: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
segments.title: Local ballroom gigs and the pay
segments.summary: The Cavaliers undercut Hartley Toots for ballrooms and clubs and shared about a dollar a man a night.

segments.chapter: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
segments.title: Ten men in one 16-cylinder Cadillac
segments.summary: The band toured when he was fourteen, packing ten players and their instruments into one Cadillac.

segments.chapter: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
segments.title: Saving for a bus and the summer route from Fort Lauderdale north
segments.summary: The band saved to buy a bus and toured every summer; at the white Trianon Ballroom they endured the toilet rule and insults, then worked up the coast and through the South.

segments.chapter: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
segments.title: Bus breaks down; stranded in Augusta at Miss Crim's hotel
segments.summary: The bus's motor fell out near Augusta; the band lived four days on stale cinnamon buns at Miss Crim's hotel and played a dance for repair money.

segments.chapter: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
segments.title: Athens bus payment and a hungry night in Alabama with a Lunceford record
segments.summary: They scraped together the bus payments at a University of Georgia dance, then ate on credit in Alabama while Jimmie Lunceford played on the jukebox.

segments.chapter: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
segments.title: Mr. Douglas's hotel in Macon and the honesty of musicians' debts
segments.summary: Hotel owners in Macon and elsewhere let stranded kids owe them, and the band paid back what it owed.

segments.chapter: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
segments.title: Caring landladies for show people: Uncle Henry, Mom Sutton and others
segments.summary: Hinton and Francis recall the people in each town who fed and housed traveling musicians.

segments.chapter: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
segments.title: Catching gonorrhea at fifteen and Ivan Rolay
segments.summary: The youngest in every band, he wanted to be a man and proudly showed Ivan Rolay his first dose of gonorrhea.

segments.chapter: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
segments.title: His mother taking his earnings
segments.summary: His mother kept every nickel he made and spent it on bills and numbers while the other boys bought clothes.

segments.title: Being turned away by Bill Rivers and Hartley Toots, 1938
segments.summary: After Earl Hines played Miami, he asked Bill Rivers for a place in Hartley Toots's band and was told to go home to his mother.

segments.title: Moving to Tampa to join Charlie Bradford's Florida Collegians
segments.summary: George Kelly broke up their band and got him a drum job in Tampa with the Florida Collegians.

segments.title: Writing to his estranged father and leaving Tampa
segments.summary: With work slow, he wrote his father in New York, who sent a bus ticket and five dollars.

segments.title: Two days by bus to New York and meeting his father
segments.summary: The bus trip north, the missing front porches in Richmond, and his father meeting him at the 50th Street bus terminal.

segments.title: First night in Harlem, jamming at the Rennie, Jocks and the 721 Club
segments.summary: He sat in at several Harlem clubs, and first saw Jabbo Smith at the 721 Club.

segments.title: The Masopeka jam session and joining Tab Smith at the Rosebud
segments.summary: He heard Lips Page and Roy Eldridge, and Tab Smith hired him for the non-union Rosebud in Brooklyn; Hinton notes the company he met.

segments.title: Meeting Cozy Cole, Les Paul and Charlie Christian
segments.summary: On his third night he heard Cozy Cole at a club on 142nd Street and played behind Les Paul and Charlie Christian.

segments.title: Hinton on how Cozy Cole replaced Leroy Maxey in Cab Calloway's band
segments.summary: Hinton explains Cab wanted a drum soloist like Gene Krupa, which brought Cozy Cole in.

segments.title: The Rhythm Club, Kaiser Marshall and other musicians from Florida
segments.summary: He visited the Rhythm Club and met Kaiser Marshall, Cedric Wallace and Cookie Mason.

segments.title: A letter from Bill Rivers after the New York news reached Miami
segments.summary: Bill Rivers wrote inviting him to join Hartley Toots's band, a letter he never answered but keeps.

segments.title: Kaiser Marshall's cymbal work, and awe at meeting his heroes
segments.summary: They discuss Kaiser Marshall as a great cymbal man and dresser, and Francis recalls stuttering from excitement.

segments.title: How his father paid for his Local 802 union membership
segments.summary: Facing a union threat at the Rosebud, his father arranged a night shift on the WPA and claimed sick pay to raise the $54.

segments.chapter: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Playing hotels with Billy Hicks and his Sizzler Six
segments.summary: He joined Billy Hicks's sextet, playing St. Regis, Astor and Waldorf rooms.

segments.chapter: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Learning to play an Apollo show from Tom Whaley
segments.summary: Unable to read music, he faked his way through the first Apollo show until conductor Tom Whaley told him to keep his foot off the bass drum and follow the lead.

segments.chapter: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Tom Whaley, Ellington's copyist, and Joe Benjamin
segments.summary: Hinton describes Whaley's knowledge of Ellington's scores and his protege Joe Benjamin; Francis promises to visit the blind Whaley.

segments.chapter: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Jam sessions and Roy Eldridge asking him to join
segments.summary: He hunted jam sessions, and Roy Eldridge, whose drummer was leaving for Chick Webb's band, offered him a job at the Arcadia.

segments.chapter: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Joining Roy's band and being christened Panama
segments.summary: His first week with Roy, the hat prompted the name Panama, which stuck; only people who knew him before 1939 call him David.

segments.chapter: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Roy defends him against manager Joe Glaser, who wanted Sid Catlett
segments.summary: At the Arcadia, a $50-a-week job, Roy stood up for his young drummer; Roy and Clyde Hart pushed him to learn to read.

segments.chapter: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: End of Reel 1 and start of Reel 2
segments.summary: Reel change and Smithsonian header for Reel 2.

segments.chapter: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: First recording with Roy Eldridge: Muskrat Ramble and High Society
segments.summary: Learning to read music, and his first recording, on Vocalion, with Don Redman arrangements.

segments.chapter: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Hinton in Orlando: a new session at Francis's home
segments.summary: Hinton states the date and location and talks about Francis's upcoming Michael's Pub engagement.

segments.chapter: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Nine months with Roy: the Arcadia, a tour to Detroit and the Apollo
segments.summary: The Arcadia's waltz-tango-jazz format, broadcasts, the Graystone Ballroom in Detroit, and a full Apollo show.

segments.title: Auditioning for Lucky Millinder at the Savoy
segments.summary: Trevor Bacon recruits him; he outplays Shadow Wilson at a Savoy audition and wins the job.

segments.title: Sister Tharpe and the Panoram film at the Savoy
segments.summary: Working the Savoy with Lucky, Sister Rosetta Tharpe joins the band, and he appears in a Panoram film short for $15.

segments.title: Savoy scale versus Arcadia pay, and Lucky's nightly pay
segments.summary: The Savoy paid $33 a week against the Arcadia's $50, but Lucky paid $11 a night on tour.

segments.title: Chitlin-circuit one-nighters and a racial insult in Goldsboro
segments.summary: Three months without a night off on the black circuit, and a hostess announcing 'a hot nigger band' in Goldsboro, North Carolina.

segments.title: Personnel of Lucky Millinder's band
segments.summary: He lists the band members around 1941, including Bill Doggett, Trevor Bacon, George Duvivier and Tab Smith.

segments.title: Clyde Hart and Freddie Webster: the breathing marks arrangement
segments.summary: Clyde Hart's arrangement of A Sinner Kissed an Angel, with Freddie Webster teaching the band to breathe together.

segments.title: Six years with Lucky, constant fights, and credit as David Francis
segments.summary: He stayed six years though he and Lucky argued weekly, and early records list him as David Francis.

segments.title: Leading his own band at the Savoy in 1946, then Willie Bryant
segments.summary: Mr. Buchanan promised a house-band slot, but Tab Smith's group got it and he lost money.

segments.title: Joining Cab Calloway and recording The Hi-De-Ho Man
segments.summary: Hired when Kansas Fields left, he played on the film soundtrack and a first Cab record date, and remembers Cab's speech 'Get what you need'.

segments.title: Cab Calloway as the greatest education: discipline and sending money home
segments.summary: Coming from Lucky's wild band, he watched Cab's veterans wire money home first, and Cab took him aside about his family.

segments.title: The first Pullman berth and seniority in Cab's band
segments.summary: New men got upper berths; he spent five minutes figuring out how to climb into his on his first night.

segments.title: Cab's strict punctuality and Francis's dream of playing with Duke
segments.summary: Cab's businesslike bandstand taught him to be on time; he had listened to Duke on a crystal set in Miami and later replaced Louis Bellson.

segments.title: A week in Duke Ellington's lax band and quitting over unpaid salary
segments.summary: After Cab's discipline, Duke's undermanned, late-starting band and half pay made him quit after a week.

segments.title: Marrying childhood sweetheart Helen Dean and their daughters
segments.summary: He married Helen Dean, whose uncle was Cedric Wallace; they had daughters Naomi and Eileen and stayed together 25 years.

segments.title: Buying a grocery store for security after reading Dan Burley's column
segments.summary: Having read of musicians ending up broke, he bought a grocery store in the Bronx for security.

segments.title: The breakup of his marriage and his weakness for women
segments.summary: He nearly had a breakdown after the divorce; he did not drink or smoke pot much but chased women until joining Cab.

segments.title: Carrying his drums through the rain between record dates
segments.summary: After a Joe Turner date at Fulton Studio he could not get a cab and walked his drums to Capitol Studio in the rain.

segments.title: Buying his first car and teaching himself to drive
segments.summary: He decided to buy a 1953 Ford, had a neighbour drive it home, then learned to drive in ten days.

segments.title: Meeting Iris Lewin at the Central Plaza
segments.summary: After the split he met social worker Iris Lewin, sister of a customer, while house drummer at the Central Plaza.

segments.title: Leaving home after a violent night and being locked out
segments.summary: After four record dates he came home to a drunk, accusing wife, left for the YMCA and found the locks changed.

segments.title: Three years of crying on Iris's shoulder; marrying her in 1970
segments.summary: Iris helped him through the breakup; he left Dinah Shore's employ to marry her in 1970.

segments.title: Getting into rhythm-and-blues dates via Leroy Kirkland and Joe Marshall
segments.summary: Leroy Kirkland and Joe Marshall brought him into New York rock and roll sessions, where his church rhythms fit.

segments.title: Touring South America with Cab and leading a band there in 1954
segments.summary: Hinton recalls the 1951 Montevideo tour with Cab; Francis took a sextet back in 1954 and became the featured band.

segments.title: Clyde Otis demo sessions and Mercury
segments.summary: Hinton recalls Francis bringing him into Clyde Otis's demo group with Bedford Hendrix arrangements.

segments.title: Peggy Sue, Otis Blackwell's Presley demos and Bobby Darin
segments.summary: He played on Buddy Holly's Peggy Sue in New York, Otis Blackwell demos that Presley copied, and Bobby Darin's Splish Splash.

segments.title: Hit records: Platters, Brook Benton, Ray Charles and Colonel Bogie's March
segments.summary: He lists hits he drummed on, and how a snare on a timpani gave Mitch Miller a field-drum sound.

segments.title: Perez Prado's Patricia and the invention of its overdubbed rhythm
segments.summary: He saved producer Herman Diaz's job by suggesting a rhythm for overdubbing onto Prado's tapes.

segments.title: Arrangers, Clyde Otis and the rhythm section deciding the groove
segments.summary: They name the arrangers and Clyde Otis hits like Ramblin' Rose; Hinton says Francis led the rhythm section.

segments.title: Atlantic Records beginnings and his failed push for a black-owned label
segments.summary: He tried to become a producer and to get Mickey Baker and others to start their own record company.

segments.title: Why the calls stopped around 1964 and Gary Chester's arrival
segments.summary: His home troubles hurt his studio work and Gary Chester's Latin-influenced style replaced his church rhythms.

segments.title: The fender bass takeover and Wilbur Bascomb
segments.summary: Hinton says the fender bass replaced him; they mention Bob Bushnell and the young Bascomb.

segments.title: Black arrangers and pioneers: Teacho Wiltshire, Bill Sanford, Jesse Stone, Leroy Kirkland
segments.summary: They praise arrangers who shaped rock and roll and rhythm-and-blues, especially Jesse Stone and Leroy Kirkland.

segments.title: New session in Orlando
segments.summary: Hinton marks a continuation of the interview.

segments.title: Whether jazz will come back and why rock and roll lasted
segments.summary: Francis thought rock would fade but notes people could dance to it, and expects jazz to return to rhythm fundamentals.

segments.title: Career resume and the General Motors Cadillac industrial shows
segments.summary: Hinton reads his resume; he toured with the GM Cadillac industrial show from 1963 to 1966.

segments.title: Dinah Shore's personal drummer
segments.summary: He calls working for Dinah Shore the best job of his life and tells how she forgave him for missing a show in Houston.

segments.title: No military service: turned down for stuttering
segments.summary: He was rejected for the draft because of his stutter, but played army camps with Lucky.

segments.title: End of Reel 2 and start of Reel 3
segments.summary: End of proceedings and Reel 3 header.

segments.title: Lucky Millinder's coffin-like sleeping bus
segments.summary: Lucky had a bus converted into beds too low to stand in, which the band rebelled against.

segments.chapter: Gambling, Cab's small groups and Havana
segments.title: Lucky Millinder's perfect four at a crap game and his spiritualist side
segments.summary: At a Charleston station Lucky made a hard four first roll on someone else's dice; Francis says he was psychic and worked as Professor Wilson, a spiritualist, in the South.

segments.chapter: Gambling, Cab's small groups and Havana
segments.title: Crap games, the Ink Spots package and sandpapered dice
segments.summary: Hinton and Francis trade stories of constant dice games; Bill Kinney of the Ink Spots kept Francis broke and his sanded dice backfired.

segments.chapter: Gambling, Cab's small groups and Havana
segments.title: The blackjack game that lost his suit money, and the end of his gambling
segments.summary: Paid at the Adams Theatre in Newark, he dealt blackjack to Lucky and others, lost his pay, and came home to tell his wife there would be no suits.

segments.chapter: Gambling, Cab's small groups and Havana
segments.title: Personnel of Cab Calloway's 1946 big band
segments.summary: Hinton and Francis name the sections of Cab's big band when Francis joined in 1946.

segments.chapter: Gambling, Cab's small groups and Havana
segments.title: Cab's seven-piece band, the Palomar Club in Vancouver and a salmon fish fry
segments.summary: After Cab cut down to seven pieces they played Vancouver, where Francis caught salmon, and later went down to four.

segments.chapter: Gambling, Cab's small groups and Havana
segments.title: The four-piece Cab Jivers in Havana and Cuban musicians
segments.summary: Playing the Montmartre in Havana, they met musicians such as Candito, Filiberto Sanchez and Chapottin.

segments.chapter: Gambling, Cab's small groups and Havana
segments.title: Havana nightlife and visiting stars
segments.summary: Francis says Havana never slept; they recall late-night food and visits from Nat Cole and Woody Herman's group.

segments.chapter: Leaving Dinah Shore and his daughters
segments.title: Leaving Dinah Shore to establish himself in Los Angeles studios
segments.summary: On Iris's urging he quit Dinah, who begged him to stay, and she got her own show soon after.

segments.chapter: Leaving Dinah Shore and his daughters
segments.title: Fathering three daughters outside marriage and deciding to search for them
segments.summary: He admits his weakness for women and decides to look for the three daughters in Los Angeles, Montreal and Newark.

segments.chapter: Leaving Dinah Shore and his daughters
segments.title: Finding his daughter Michelle in California
segments.summary: A Phoenix gig led him to the mother's brother, and he met Michelle, who had been told her father was dead.

segments.chapter: Leaving Dinah Shore and his daughters
segments.title: Tracking down daughter Penny in Montreal and Detroit
segments.summary: Using phone books, he traced Carol, learned Penny had been adopted, and met her in Detroit.

segments.chapter: Leaving Dinah Shore and his daughters
segments.title: Finding Sandra through the Platters' Tony Williams connection
segments.summary: A chain of contacts led to Sandra's mother, and he met Sandra and her six daughters in the Bronx.

segments.title: Resume of studio hits: Four Seasons, Neil Sedaka, Connie Francis, Paul Anka
segments.summary: At Hinton's urging he lists hit sessions, including the first bass drum mike on What's the Matter, Baby.

segments.title: How Patricia was built on an overdub for Perez Prado
segments.summary: Retelling the tape-overdub story: a tambourine part, bass guitar and brushes made Patricia a near million-seller.

segments.title: Roy Hamilton and the cowbell on Love Is Strange
segments.summary: Jesse Stone arranged Don't Let Go; his cowbell suggestion completed Mickey and Sylvia's Love Is Strange.

segments.title: More hits: the Platters, Jackie Wilson, Brook Benton and the Fools Rush In rhythm
segments.summary: He lists more sessions and explains he took the Fools Rush In rhythm from hillbilly rhythm guitar.

segments.title: Clyde Otis, the rhythm section and passing up contractor money
segments.summary: Clyde Otis let him set rhythms but was annoyed he gave the contracting to Frank Carroll and earned scale.

segments.title: Dinah Washington's brushes and Ray Charles teaching a gospel feel
segments.summary: On What a Difference a Day Makes he used press rolls with brushes; Ray Charles showed him the church quarter-note brush feel for Drown in My Own Tears.

segments.title: The 12/8 rhythm on I Put a Spell on You and more hits
segments.summary: Screaming Jay Hawkins's record was the first R&B date using 12/8; he lists many more sessions with Joe Turner, Buddy Holly and others.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: Bootin' tenor: Sam Taylor, Red Prysock and King Curtis's chicken sound
segments.summary: Francis describes the swinging 'bootin' tenor' sound and how King Curtis copied Sam Taylor before adding his chicken sound on Charlie Brown.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: 1974 England tour with Warren Covington and Sy Oliver
segments.summary: He toured England with Warren Covington's Tommy Dorsey band, with Sy Oliver conducting the second half.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: Ray Conniff's first album and years of touring with him
segments.summary: He devised a brush rhythm for Conniff's voices-as-horns sound and toured England, Japan and South America with him.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: Touring Japan with Sam Taylor, a star after Harlem Nocturne
segments.summary: He played 72 cities in Japan with Sam Taylor, who was the biggest name there after the Beatles.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: Band boys: Russell, Harold Holden and Rudolph Rillis
segments.summary: They recall Lucky's fashion-plate valet Russell and Cab's valets, with Rudolph Rillis the epitome of the band boy.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: Studio band boys: Freddie the Freeloader, Larry and Onesta Reese
segments.summary: They remember colorful band boys of the New York recording scene such as Freddie the Freeloader and Onesta Reese.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: Archie Bleyer's fussy studio and Business in F
segments.summary: Bleyer moved the drummer around the studio for the right sound; Hinton played his Business in F as a teenager.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: Broadway bombs, Mitch Miller TV and the Ed Sullivan show with Cab
segments.summary: He lists three failed Broadway shows, Sing Along With Mitch Miller, and Ed Sullivan appearances with Cab's four-piece band.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: First recordings with Roy Eldridge and Plucking the Bass
segments.summary: He lists the tunes from his first Roy Eldridge sessions, and Hinton recalls his own Plucking the Bass solo with Cab.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: Records with Lucky Millinder: Apollo Jump, Shout Sister Shout and others
segments.summary: He names hits with Lucky Millinder and Sister Tharpe, mostly on race labels as two-sided records.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: The Mills Blue Rhythm Band that became Lucky Millinder's
segments.summary: Hinton and Francis discuss Irving Mills's band, which Lucky fronted with Red Allen, Higginbotham and Edgar Hayes.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: Club-date and society bands beyond jazz
segments.summary: He wanted to play all kinds of music and worked with Lester Lanin, Jerry Jerome and other single-engagement bands.

segments.chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
segments.title: New York versus California and why New York is unique
segments.summary: Francis argues New York offers studios, theatres, club dates and jazz clubs, whereas California depends on studios; he calls New York America.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: Resuming on August 16: wanting a drum from age four
segments.summary: Francis restarts his story: cardboard Christmas drums that lasted a week, and the family's UNIA membership.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: End of Reel 3 and start of Reel 4
segments.summary: Cut, end of proceedings and Reel 4 header.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: UNIA Drum and Bugle Corps, St. Agnes band and the Church of God gig
segments.summary: He became top drummer of the UNIA corps by nine, then played with the UNIA and St. Agnes bands and for Sunday church services.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: First gig in 1931 and the barbecue-stand juke joint
segments.summary: His first gig was at the UNIA Hall in July 1931; then Sonny Boy hired him for a rough juke joint where the band hid behind the piano.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: Mr. Kirksey's school kids and the George McCaskel band
segments.summary: A school-kid band from Booker T. Washington High with George Kelly and others replaced drummer Vincent Augberry with him.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: First tour away from home at fourteen and the Trianon Ballroom
segments.summary: His mother entrusted him to front man Ivan Rowe; at Fort Lauderdale's Trianon the Black band waited for white men to leave the toilet.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: Replacing a bass drum head every time a drunk punched through it
segments.summary: A patron broke his bass drum head each fortnight and paid $5; he soaked and tucked new calfskin heads by hand in a wash tub.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: Wakes and funeral customs in Miami
segments.summary: The body was brought home the night before the funeral; friends sang hymns, told stories and drank all night.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: Marching in St. Agnes band funerals and stopping at the edge of White town
segments.summary: He describes snares muffled on slow dirges, musicians drinking moonshine during the service, and halting at the boundary of the white section; Hinton notes his nickname Pump.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: Lettego, cousin Harold and the first drummer who inspired him
segments.summary: He recalls a Bahamian drummer nicknamed Lettego, with a megaphone on the snare, at his father's bootleg parties, and his father's opposition to music.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: Chick Webb as idol and Kaiser Marshall's visit to Miami
segments.summary: He idolized Chick Webb from radio broadcasts, never saw him, and admired Kaiser Marshall's style.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: Ten years as house drummer at the Central Plaza alongside Zutty Singleton
segments.summary: He was house drummer at the Central Plaza with Conrad Janis's group while Zutty Singleton led the other half-hour set.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: Big Sid Catlett: first meeting in Miami in 1935 and fishing at Wildwood
segments.summary: Sid Catlett, with Don Redman's band, spent an intermission teaching him; later they hung out in California and fished at Wildwood.

segments.chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
segments.title: Count Basie's band and Joe Jones at the Famous Door
segments.summary: He first saw Basie's band at the Rockland Palace in 1938 and met drummer Joe Jones in 1939, calling him the sparkplug.

segments.title: Tours of Europe since 1973 and the Lucky Millinder concert in Nice
segments.summary: His first European trip was with Milt Buckner; in 1976 he led a Lucky Millinder tribute at Carnegie Hall and Nice.

segments.title: European audiences and traveling conditions
segments.summary: He says he is a king in Europe and 'Panama Who?' at home; he found transport poor but hotels good.

segments.title: Plans for the future and jazz as dance music
segments.summary: He will work as leader or sideman wherever the money is, and insists jazz should be danceable.

segments.title: Advice to young drummers
segments.summary: He tells young drummers to learn their instrument, learn to read and always arrive early.

segments.title: Cozy Cole's lessons at the Krupa-Cole drum school
segments.summary: He took lessons for about four months with Cozy Cole at the Gene Krupa and Cozy Cole school on Eighth Avenue and learned rudiments.

segments.title: Final thoughts and thanks to Hinton
segments.summary: Francis says the interview was a pleasure and recalls telling Hinton he would retire at his age yet still feels he is learning.

segments.title: Closing contact details and end of tape
segments.summary: Hinton asks for Francis's identification and addresses for the archive; the recording ends.
